articles.title: Develop Healthy Tech Habits with Your Teen
articles.summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
articles.summary_zh: 每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。 我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。
articles.title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
articles.content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. He says, “In any royal palace, you’re sure to find soldiers keeping watch over who and what has access to the very important king or queen inside”; those guards, he contends, are our habits, and “the strength of the soldiers determines how protected the palace is” (158). Early in the book, James calls teens to learn discernment. As he unpacks this habit, he warns them away from the siren song of social media influencers who question parental authority: “When an online influencer who doesn’t know you or care for you speaks about your parents or mentors in a way that makes you want to trust those people less and the influencer more, that’s a massive sign that what you’re listening to is false” (44). Yet James doesn’t merely tell young people to flee digital technology’s dangers; he also beckons them to put on habits that will help them cultivate virtue, in-person friendship, accountability, industrious work, creativity, and rest. For Parents Too Many of these habits are relational. In his introduction, for example, James encourages teens to read his book with a parent, teacher, pastor, or mentor. The discussion questions he includes at the end of each chapter make this counsel practical. This counsel is also wise, because while Scroll Less, Live More is a book for teens, it’s a book for parents too. As a parent and youth worker, I found James’s encouragement to develop a habit of self-awareness convicting. He calls readers to pay attention when being online leads to feelings of anger, anxiety, or boredom so that you know when to “log off and touch grass.” Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia : “Spiritual laziness that causes you to fill up on meaningless things so much that you cannot delight in God” (65). He nailed me. How many times do I fill life’s quiet moments—waiting in a line, a few minutes between meetings, or sadly even lulls in conversation—by pulling out my phone instead of being attentive to nature, the people around me, and the Lord? Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia . I can get frustrated when I see this tendency in teens, but as Brett McCracken writes , “What parents model with our own devices ultimately matters more than what we say to our kids about them.” James’s book helped me see ways I’ve failed to fight endless scrolling in my own life. As parents, we need God’s Spirit to help us grow in self-awareness about our tech habits. We need his grace to help us confess those failures to the teens we parent and lead. And we need a heart of wisdom and phone-stack intentionality, not just at youth group meetings but throughout our lives. Scroll Less, Live More helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
articles.content_zh:
每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。
我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。 这帮助了我们团体的学生更密切地关注彼此和圣经文本。 在他实用的新书"Scroll Less"(Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Health Tech Habits for Teens)中,塞缪尔·詹姆斯称赞了一些类似的做法.
他的目标是让青少年 " 生动地了解在当今数字时代将[圣经上 智慧应用于技术应用的外表 " (155)。 詹姆斯认识到简单、可重复的做法可以帮助年轻人抵制当今技术推广的愚蠢,让他们在上帝的恐惧中成长。
Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More 在他的前作中为成年人奠定的基础上, 科技并非中立。 而是一股强大的力量, “塑造并影响我们,
技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 为了说明这个事实,詹姆斯指出19世纪发明的技术: 在电话之前, 人们刚刚接受, 如果他们不和别人在同一间屋子里,
在电话引入后,能够随时与另一个地方的某个人通信不仅成为可能,而且非常重要.
(125) 同样地,21世纪的技术,如基因人工智能,也带来了新的可能性和更大的期望: " 人工智能在人类很少直接参与的情况下生产出惊人的作品和艺术的能力,使人们期望经常用于这些目的是正常的 " (127)。 我们越是放弃我们的创造力和努力,我们就越相信我们应该这样做。
技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 数字技术也以其他方式改变我们。 James借鉴了Neil Postman、Nicholas Carr、Marshall McLuhan等科技现实主义者的作品, 詹姆斯反复地向年轻人展示,不良的数字习惯如何影响他们的认知,情感和关系.
生活在电话里会减缓思考, 让青少年感到焦虑甚至愤怒, 智慧之道:守护你的心 我们如何帮助年轻人避免这条道路? 詹姆斯给青少年一些实际的鼓励,让他们在一夜之间在卧室以外的地方充电电话.
他还提供了一份自查问题清单,帮助他们提高自我意识,他呼吁遵守家庭规则,例如只在家庭的空地使用装置。 但最终,詹姆斯相信,使用良好的技术不仅仅涉及遵循一个做和不做的清单。
他写道, 我们不需要一连串的规则, 每次苹果公司发布新手机或新社交媒体应用时, 我们需要智慧。 (16-17) 普罗活佛说:"对耶和华的恐惧是智慧的开始,对圣者的知识是洞察力"(9:10).
詹姆斯明白,智慧和上帝的知识的不断增长,不仅需要调整一个人的屏幕时间设置,还需要守护一个人的心。 詹姆斯鼓励青少年将心想成一个国王或女王所居住的宫殿. 他说,“在任何皇家宫殿里,你肯定能找到士兵来监视谁和什么人可以接触到里面非常重要的国王或女王”;
他认为,这些警卫是我们的习惯,“士兵的力量决定了宫殿的保护程度”(158)。 在书的早期,詹姆斯召集少年来学习辨识.
当他解开这种习惯时,他警告他们不要听那些质疑父母权威的社交媒体影响者所唱的警笛:“当一个不了解你或关心你的网络影响者以一种方式谈论你的父母或导师,使你更希望信任这些人,而影响者更多,这是你所听到的都是虚假的大规模迹象”(44)。
但詹姆斯并不只是告诉年轻人逃离数字技术的危险;他还诱使他们树立习惯,帮助他们培养美德、亲身友谊、责任感、勤奋的工作、创造力和休息。 对于父母来说,这些习惯中有许多是相互关联的。
例如,在介绍中,詹姆斯鼓励青少年与家长,教师,牧师,或导师一起阅读他的书. 他在每个章节结尾处包括的讨论问题使该律师成为实际。 这本书也是明智的, 因为虽然《Less Scroll》,
作为父母和青年工作者,我发现詹姆斯鼓励培养一种自我认识定罪的习惯。
他呼吁读者关注网络引发愤怒、焦虑或无聊的感觉, Listless boorom是Acedia罪的一种形式:“导致你充斥无意义的事物而不能对上帝取悦的原始懒惰”(65)。 他钉住我。
我有多少次在静静的瞬间, 等待一行, 几分钟的会面, 无名无姓的无聊是阿塞迪亚罪的一种形式
但正如Brett McCracken所写 的 , “ 父母用我们自己的设备建模最终比我们对孩子说的更重要。 ” 詹姆士的书帮助我看到了自己一生中一直未能与无尽的卷轴斗争的方式。 作为父母,我们需要上帝的精神来帮助我们增强对技术习惯的自我意识。
我们需要他的恩典来帮助我们 向那些我们父母和领导的孩子承认这些失败 我们需要一个智慧的心脏 和电话袋的故意, 不仅在青年小组会议上,而且我们一生。 Scroll Less, Live More帮助青少年和家长发展他们所需要的技术技能,以过着根植于现实并充满智慧的生活.

articles.title: Effective Altruists and the Spreadsheet Gospel
articles.summary: Effective altruism commands us to love our neighbor yet dissolves that neighbor into a statistic. It asks for the fruit of the image of God while denying the root.
articles.summary_zh: 过去十年来,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷扎根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是因为它的想法决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。 《经济学家》最近将哲学称为“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称该运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。
articles.title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
articles.content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it. As a Christian and tech-policy analyst based in Washington, DC, where many of these conversations are taking place, I want to explain what effective altruism is, examine what it promises and where it fails to deliver, and show why this budding movement is incongruent with and a poor substitute for the gospel. What Is Effective Altruism? Effective altruism emerged in the late 2000s and early 2010s from the convergence of several intellectual movements, particularly utilitarian philosophy and evidence-based philanthropy. Australian academic Peter Singer provided an important foundation with his 1972 essay “ Famine, Affluence and Morality ,” where he argues that people have a moral obligation to prevent suffering when they can do so at relatively little cost to themselves. At its core, effective altruism is consequentialist, judging the rightness of an action chiefly by its outcomes. The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The Centre for Effective Altruism explains , “We’re committed to prioritizing actions that benefit more lives over actions that benefit a few—that saving a billion lives is more important than saving ten.” The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The movement took shape with the founding of several philanthropic organizations, such as GiveWell and 80,000 Hours . These groups emphasize measuring charitable impact, directing money toward the most effective actions, and choosing “high-impact” careers based on their potential to do good. Their approach to charitable giving has produced endeavors to improve global health , animal welfare , and economic disparities , among other areas. Over the past decade, effective altruism has expanded its scope, focusing on posterity and “longtermism,” the belief that “positively influencing the longterm future is a key moral priority of our time.” The Economist notes a belief this leads to: “Those not born yet should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are ‘longtermists’ who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.” This belief manifests itself in a focus on concerns such as existential risk (e.g., climate change or the next pandemic), nuclear proliferation, and artificial intelligence. For many in Silicon Valley, advanced AI is the defining problem of our day. The concern about a potential AI apocalypse explains why the movement has invested heavily in AI research, AI companies, and AI advocacy and safety. It’s not difficult to see why this philosophy has a natural audience among AI researchers and Silicon Valley tech luminaries. Effective altruism enables technologists to approach ethics in a way that can feel familiar: a series of probabilities, tradeoffs, and expected results—measuring an individual’s moral standing as mathematic calculations, similar to the process of building a software program where different inputs result in varied outputs. For ambitious individuals accustomed to solving complicated projects through ingenuity and critical analysis, this movement delivers reassuring community in an industry that often feels isolating. Adherents have a sense of higher purpose and calling as they’re suddenly confronted with extraordinary individual wealth and wrestle with the consequences of their technological discoveries. It’s hard to describe effective altruism without addressing its more eccentric views, some of which divide the movement itself. For example, the focus on animal welfare has led many in the movement to believe that any and all sentient beings share the same moral value, including but not limited to shrimp . Yes, since a dollar can go a long way to protect the well-being of a single crustacean , this cause could be the most efficient use of charitable giving. Notably, the effective altruist community has also drawn scrutiny for its sexual culture. A 2023 Time investigation highlighted how the movement’s overwhelmingly male membership, heavy overlap between work and home life, and its subculture of polyamory (which some have promoted as more rational than monogamy) has created a “culture of sexual harassment and abuse.” These dynamics have caused many—including Christians—to be concerned about the group’s outsize influence on culture. What Effective Altruism Promises (and Fails to Deliver) Effective altruism’s turn toward longtermism promises that the right people, armed with the right understanding of the stakes, can steer humanity safely through an uncertain future. Many in this community believe their adherence to consequentialism and longtermism gives them a special moral qualification to shape public policy. In their own eyes, effective altruists are the men and women of the hour. This conviction has moved from theory into practice. Political engagement by adherents has increased both on the public stage and backstage through building and funding civil society institutions to influence policymakers to embrace their ideology. One of the movement’s most prominent figures (though he has denied belonging to it), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, has been leaning on this philosophy to guide his leadership of his company and shape his approach to the future of AI . Yet for all its ambition, the movement struggles to deliver on what it promises. Effective altruism’s confidence in its own reasoning to navigate the future is a hubristic claim to possess unprecedented human knowledge. Any ethic that judges right and wrong by outcomes assumes we can reliably know what our actions will produce. It treats the future as a closed system of causes and effects that the right person or algorithm can calculate. But human knowledge is finite. We can’t trace the full effects of a single choice, much less forecast the welfare of billions of potential lives. At best, an outcome-based ethic can render its moral verdict only in hindsight. Most fundamentally, effective altruism fails us because it’s an ethic without a moral foundation. It has a laudable premise: Too many people around the globe are suffering, and those with means should help. Adherents can accurately quantify certain societal woes and calculate which actions could most efficiently produce the greatest benefit. But the philosophy largely assumes the moral obligations on which those calculations depend. In Singer’s foundational essay, he uses an illustration of a man wearing expensive sneakers who walks past a drowning child. He does a moral calculation that it’s better to save the child even if it ruins his shoes. The illustration works only because we already know the child matters and that walking past would be monstrous. But a strictly consequentialist framework can’t tell us why . If people are ultimately containers of welfare to be added up, then no one has worth in himself. Each matters only as a quantity in a calculation. And who decides which quantities count? Without an external source of moral truth, the answer is ultimately the individual. Each effective altruist must reason his way to his own conclusion about what “the most good” is, and no authority outside himself can tell him he’s wrong. Taken to its logical end, this leaves room for almost anything

过去十年来,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷扎根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是因为它的想法决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。
《经济学家》最近将哲学称为“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称该运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。 即使这种哲学正在推动市场和形成全球辩论,许多基督徒对它并不熟悉。
作为总部设在华盛顿特区的基督教和技术政策分析者,我想解释一下这些对话是何等有效的利他主义,审视它所承诺的以及它未能实现之处,并表明为什么这个萌芽的运动与福音是不一致的,并且是一个糟糕的替代物。 什么是有效的异端主义?
有效的利他主义在2000年代末和2010年代初从几个知识运动,特别是功利主义哲学和基于证据的慈善运动的趋同中出现.
澳大利亚学者Peter Singer以他1972年的论文“饥荒、富裕和道德”为重要基础,他认为,当人们能够以相对较少的代价来预防痛苦时,他们有道德义务。 有效的利他主义的核心是结果主义,主要根据其结果判断行动是否正确。
有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥他们在社会中的优势。
有效替代主义中心解释说,“我们致力于优先考虑有利于更多生命的行动,而不是有利于少数人的行动——拯救十亿生命比拯救十亿生命更重要。 ” 有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥他们在社会中的优势。
这场运动随着多个慈善组织的成立而成形, 这些团体强调衡量慈善影响,将资金用于最有效的行动,并根据他们做好事的潜力选择“影响大”的职业。
他们的慈善捐赠方法 带来了改善全球健康、动物福利和经济差距的努力。
在过去的十年中,有效的利他主义扩大了它的范围,把重点放在后代和“长期主义”上,认为“积极影响长期未来是我们时代的关键道德优先事项”。 《经济学家》指出,这导致了一种信念:“那些尚未出生的人应该得到平衡的权衡——而且可能有数万亿。
许多职业介绍所是“长期主义者 ” , 他们认为他们有义务在遥远的将来防范风险, 即使这让今天的美好事业饿死, 这种信念表现在关注存在风险(如气候变化或下一个大流行病)、核扩散和人工智能。
对硅谷的许多人来说,先进的AI是我们当今的决定性问题. 对潜在的AI启示录的担忧解释了为何该运动在AI研究,AI公司,AI倡导和安全方面投入了大量资金. 为何这个哲学在AI研究者和硅谷科技流派中拥有自然的读者,
有效的利他主义使技术专家能够以能够感到熟悉的方式处理伦理问题:一系列概率、权衡和预期结果——衡量个人的道德地位作为数学计算,类似于建立软件程序的过程,不同投入导致不同的产出。
对于那些习惯于通过智慧和批判性分析来解决复杂项目的野心勃勃的个人来说,这一运动在一个常常感到孤立的行业中为社区带来安慰。 坚持者有更高的目标感, 并召唤他们突然面对非凡的个人财富,
很难描述有效的利他主义, 例如,对动物福利的重视使得运动中许多人相信,任何和所有神灵生物都具有同样的道德价值,包括但不限于虾。
是的,由于一美元对保护单一甲壳类动物的福祉可以发挥很大的作用,因此这一事业可能是慈善捐赠的最有效用途。 值得注意的是,有效的利他主义社区也对其性文化进行了审查。
2023年的一项时间调查凸显了该运动绝大多数男性成员、工作和家庭生活之间的严重重叠、以及其多元文化(有些人提倡这种文化比一夫一妻制更合理)如何创造了“性骚扰和虐待文化 ” 。 这些动态导致包括基督徒在内的许多人担心该团体对文化的影响过大。
有效的利他主义向长期主义的转变会保证,以正确理解利害关系为武装的正确人民能够安全地引导人类渡过不确定的未来。 这个社区中许多人认为,他们坚持后果主义和长期主义,使他们具有制定公共政策的特殊道德资格。
在他们自己的眼里,有效的利他主义者是时空的男女. 这种信念已经从理论转变为实践。 通过建立和资助民间社会机构影响决策者接受其意识形态,信徒们在公共舞台和后台的政治参与有所增加。
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei(虽然他否认自己属于这个运动)最知名的人物之一, 然而,运动的雄心壮志却在努力兑现它的承诺。
有效的利他主义相信它自己的通向未来的推理,是一种傲慢地宣称拥有前所未有的人类知识。 根据结果判断对错的任何道德都假定我们能够可靠地知道我们的行动将产生什么。 它把未来当作一个封闭的因果系统,由正确的人或算法来计算. 但人类的知识是有限的。
我们无法追踪单一选择的全部效果, 充其量,基于结果的伦理只有在事后才能作出道德判断。 最根本的,有效的利他主义使我们失望,因为它是一种没有道德基础的伦理。
它有一个值得称赞的前提:全球有太多的人在受苦,那些有手段的人应该提供帮助。 坚持者可以准确地量化某些社会灾难,并计算哪些行动能够最有效地产生最大的利益。 但哲学基本上承担了这些计算所依赖的道德义务。
在Singer的奠基论文中,他用一个插图说明一名穿昂贵运动鞋的人走过一个溺水的孩子. 他做了一个道德的计算,认为救孩子更好, 插图之所以有效,只是因为我们已经知道儿童的重要性,而且走过去将是可怕的。 但严格地说,
如果人们最终是福利的容器 被加起来, 那么没有人值得自己。 每种物质在计算中仅作为数量。 谁决定数量是多少? 没有道德真理的外部来源,答案最终是个人.
每一个有效的利他主义者必须解释自己对什么是“最美好”的结论, 任何外部权威都不能告诉他自己错了。 顺理成章地说,这为几乎一切留下了空间

articles.content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. The playlist has 30 songs (one for each of November’s 30 days) expressing gratitude to God for our salvation in Christ, for the many blessings of marriage and family, and for the beauty of the earth. articles.title: Your Church May Know Less Bible Than You Think (And What to Do About It)
articles.summary: A new survey indicates Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it.
articles.summary_zh: 1900年11月,马克·吐温向康涅狄格韦斯利安大学的学生发表了题为“文学失踪”的演讲。 他对他们说:「我不相信你们谁读过失乐园, 这是你想要信任的东西。 这是. 一个经典的定义——人人都想读,没有人想读。
articles.title_zh: 你的教会可能知道的圣经比你想象的要少（以及该怎么做）
articles.content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. When asked their first priority in discipleship, the largest number responded that it be “biblical knowledge focused.” And in response to the question “What approaches does your church specifically use to disciple and encourage the spiritual development of adults in your congregation?” 89 percent responded the sermon, the top answer by a 20-point gap, with adult Sunday school listed second. The sermon matters enormously. But we’re learning that the sermon alone cannot do the heavy lifting of solving the Bible literacy crisis. It’s a passive learning environment, a one-way communication. Imagine if your local public school believed passively listening to a lecture was the only way to form students into contributing citizens. Why does the local church think people comprehensively learn the Bible in such settings? Imagine also if your local public school recommended peer-led discussion groups as a primary vehicle for educating students. Imagine if the time spent in these groups was used to reflect for 30 minutes or so on what was taught in a lecture several days before: Mrs. Harker lectures on the quadratic equation for 30 minutes on Monday; students discuss how to apply the quadratic equation to their lives for 30 minutes on Wednesday. Who’s passing an algebra exam? Yet, 95 percent of pastors surveyed responded that discipleship isn’t completed in a program but in a relationship. Hence, the ubiquity of the community-group model in evangelical churches. We Know What to Do The wildest part of this disconnect about how to teach what’s good in a way that sticks is that we know the answer. The answer isn’t a new thing but an old thing recently forgotten. The church must return to its roots as the solver of illiteracy, both within its walls and also without. Education pastors can be tempted to dabble, trying one thing or another to see what their church members might find interesting, buying the latest study from a Christian publisher on the assumption it’s good. The idea that there are well-attested best practices for Christian education seems to have gotten lost. Just like a healthy local school, churches need to reclaim active, dedicated learning environments—spaces designated explicitly for the purpose of teaching the Bible. They need to think like educators: What is the scope and sequence for what we’ll teach? And they need to ask a better question than “What do my congregants want to learn?” I didn’t want to learn grammar, but thank goodness, Mrs. Wagner knew I needed it and taught it to me anyway. Her evident enthusiasm for the topic fascinated me. What was I missing that she knew? I learned grammar in a dialogic space taught by a subject-matter expert with an evident love for her subject. That love was contagious. Imagine if the church taught people the Bible like Mrs. Wagner taught grammar. It might become the classic of classics that every Christian actually wants to read. Christians possess the most beautiful and compelling book of all. Because a book forms the foundation of our faith, Christians have always been invested in solving illiteracy. We’ve striven to train people to read because reading is essential to the promulgation of our faith. The roots of public education and university systems lie in Christian efforts to grow literacy. The availability of vernacular translations of the Bible is the result of a concern for readability for all. Sunday school began in the late 1700s as an effort to educate children who worked in factories prior to child labor laws, seizing their one day off work as a literacy opportunity. Christians have been literacy champions in previous dark ages—and Christians can be again. Don’t Look Away In the first article I ever wrote for The Gospel Coalition back in 2012, I considered the Bible literacy crisis: “Why does biblical ignorance continue to dog the church, despite the good intentions of leadership to obey the Great Command to make disciples? I believe the answer lies in our definition of a disciple. A disciple is, literally, a learner—one who follows another’s teaching.” Fourteen years later, I’m still asking church leaders to remember to teach learners as the most basic function of discipleship, and to do so with proven tools. Don’t look away from the problem. Don’t tell yourself it’s the problem of the church down the road. In a cultural literacy freefall, all churches will feel the negative effects in Bible liter

1900年11月,马克·吐温向康涅狄格韦斯利安大学的学生发表了题为“文学失踪”的演讲。 他对他们说:「我不相信你们谁读过失乐园, 这是你想要信任的东西。 这是.
一个经典的定义——人人都想读,没有人想读。” Twain注意到文盲的起步, 我们在智能手机和社交媒体时代所看到的统计数据证明了我们被侵蚀的识字率: 2003年,15岁以上的美国人平均每天读取21.9分。
至2010年已降至18.3分,2025年已下沉至每天16.2分. 想象一下ChatGPT在未来几年里会如何进一步切断这个数字. 美国正在迅速进入一个后文化的现实, 一种新的黑暗时代, 在其中,我们消耗信息 在图像和声音叮咬, 这一切都被其他人预想。
考虑一下对一种信仰体系的影响,这种信仰体系的代代相传被放在一本书上。 基督教识字危机 生活之路研究的一项新调查使基督教对《圣经》的承诺和对《圣经》的了解之间的裂痕大为缓解。
在典型的一个月内参加教堂的基督徒有2000多人接受过8个类别的圣经知识调查:主要人物、经文、活动、圣经的分化等等。 研究人员围绕什么是通常众所周知的而不是模糊的问题。 3个受访者中有2个得分不足60分,成绩不及格.
百分之五十五无法正确命名以色列第一任国王. 只有11%的人可以正确订购四起"旧约"重大事件,只有27%的人可以正确订购四起"新约"重大事件. 百分之四十四未能将"马克"一书认定为属于"福音".
三分之二的受访者错误地认为"赫泽基亚"是"圣经"一书,44%的人认为"托马斯福音"也是". 基督教徒已经屈服于文化的普遍识字危机. " 书生"不读. 圣经本身,是所有经典的经典,显然已经成为了每个基督徒都想阅读的一本书,很少有基督徒想阅读.
如果我们真的读到来维持我们的信仰,我们更可能阅读有关圣经的书籍,而不是圣经本身. 我们可能会使用布道或播客, 或利用奉献资源, 挑出诗句,
散会失败 我认为这些结果表明门徒战略失败, 我们不能把自己所不知道的东西传给别人。 如果教会不能教别人观察耶稣的旨意, 数字显示我们甚至没有教授基本知识。
如果教堂是一所负责教授基本数学和阅读的当地公立学校,我们就会得到一个不及格的分数,并面临资金制裁. " 书中的人 " 不读。 然而,根据2024年对2,620名新教牧师进行的生活道研究调查,52%的人对其教会的门徒身份和精神形成状况感到满意.
29%的人报告说,他们定期评估其教会中的门徒进步。
当被问及他们在门徒中的首要地位时,人数最多的回答是“圣经知识集中”。 在回答“你的教堂对门徒具体使用什么方法,鼓励成年人在会堂中的精神发展?” 的问题时,89%的人回答布道,即最高的回答是20分的差距,成人星期日学校排在第二位。
讲道很重要 但我们知道,单凭布道并不能解决圣经的通晓危机。 这是被动的学习环境, 想象一下,如果当地的公立学校 相信被动地听一个演讲 是培养学生 贡献公民的唯一途径。
当地教会为何认为人们在这样的环境下全面学习"圣经"? 也想一想,如果你的地方公立学校建议由同行领导的讨论小组作为教育学生的主要工具。 想象一下,如果在这些团体中度过的时间被用来反思几天前在一次讲座中所教的内容:
哈克周一关于四分法方程式的讲座为30分钟;学生周三讨论如何将四分法方程式应用于他们的生活30分钟. 谁要通过代数考试? 但95%的受访牧师回应说, 门徒身份不是在一个计划中完成, 因此,福音教会中普遍存在社区团体模式。
我们知道该做什么 最疯狂的部分 如何教导什么是好 的方式坚持, 答案并不是新事物, 教堂必须恢复其根基,作为解决文盲问题的手段,无论是在其墙上还是在墙外。
教育牧师可能会被诱惑去玩弄, 尝试看他们教会成员会发现什么有趣的东西, 基督教教育方面有经过充分检验的最佳做法的想法似乎已经消失。
与健康的当地学校一样,教会需要恢复积极、专注的学习环境——明确指定用于教授圣经的空间。 他们需要像教育家一样思考: 我们将要教授的内容的范围和顺序是什么? 他们需要问一个比“我的教友们想学什么”更好的问题。 我不想学语法,但谢天谢地,夫人。
瓦格纳知道我需要它 并且教给我 她对这个话题的明显热情让我着迷. 我错过了什么 她知道? 我在一个对话空间学习了语法, 由一位主题专家教授, 爱是传染性的。 想象一下如果教会教人们像瓦格纳夫人那样教授了文法的圣经.
这可能会成为每个基督徒真正想阅读的经典. 基督徒拥有最美丽和最有说服力的书 因为一本书构成了我们信仰的基础,所以基督徒总是被投入解决文盲问题. 我们努力训练人们阅读,
公共教育和大学制度的根源在于基督教努力提高识字率。 圣经的方言翻译的可用性是关注全民可读性的结果. 星期天学校于1700年代后期开始,以努力教育那些在童工法之前在工厂工作的儿童,抓住他们一天的休息时间作为识字的机会.
基督徒在之前的黑暗时代是识字的冠军——基督徒也可以再次成为. 别走开 我在2012年为"福音联盟"撰写的第一篇文章中,认为"圣经的通晓危机":"圣经的无知为什么继续支持教会,尽管领导者有服从"大命令"让门徒成为门徒的良好意图?
我相信答案就在于我们对门徒的定义 从字面上讲,一个弟子是一个学习者——一个听从他人教导的人。 十四年后, 我仍要求教会领袖们记住, 也不要忽略问题。 别告诉自己,
在文化知识自由落地中,所有教会都会在"圣经"一升中感受到负面影响

articles.title: Does Christianity Make Sense? On God, Evil, and the Ache (with Gavin Ortlund)
articles.summary: Gavin Ortlund joins Collin Hansen to discuss apologetics and why Christianity makes sense.
articles.summary_zh: 不久前,我儿子问我 大卫国王在塞缪尔8号杀死的所有人 我们一直读这本书, 他有权被打扰。 我们曾讨论过为什么他不紧张,我们如何发展道德本能,以及我们如何回应因旧约中这些和类似说法而拒绝上帝的人。 我们一起做杂技表演 我将指向我的朋友Gavin Ortlund的YouTube频道, 然后,几年后,我将指给他看加文的著作,包括他的最新著作《基督教为何要讲道理:关于耶稣的一书、世界的谜题以及你心中的长寿》(Zondervan Reflectionive ) 。
articles.title_zh: 基督教有意义吗？论上帝、邪恶和痛苦（与Gavin Ortlund合作）
articles.content: Not long ago, my son asked me about all the people King David killed in 2 Samuel 8. We’ve been reading through that book during family devotions before bed. He’s right to be disturbed. So we had a conversation about why he’s unnerved, how we develop moral instincts, and how we’d respond to someone who rejects God because of these and similar accounts in the Old Testament. We did apologetics together. As he gets a little older, I’ll point him toward the YouTube channel of my friend Gavin Ortlund, who does an excellent job of answering many hard questions about Christianity and the Bible. Then, a few years later, I’ll point him to Gavin’s books, including his latest, Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart (Zondervan Reflective). He’s back on Gospelbound to discuss all things apologetics, from the multiverse, to slavery, to morality as merely a taste for sugar, to winning the lottery 10 billion times in a row. In This Episode 00:00 – Why people may be more open to spiritual answers today 03:36 – “The ache” and the longing for transcendence 09:29 – What about Christianity makes the least sense to Gavin? 11:39 – The problem of evil and the limits of tidy answers 19:09 – The growing challenge of divine hiddenness 24:34 – Fine-tuning and the odds of a life-permitting universe 32:07 – Is morality without God just a matter of taste? 37:25 – Slavery, the Bible, and the Christian roots of human equality 42:23 – Why fulfilled prophecy surprised Gavin 48:00 – What apologetic questions should Christians prepare for next? Resources Mentioned: Why Christianity Makes Sense by Gavin Ortlund Mere Christianity by C. S. Lewis Making Sense of God by Timothy Keller The Reason for God by Timothy Keller The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoevsky Bullies and Saints by John Dickson Dominion by Tom Holland Gavin Ortlund’s YouTube channel, “ Truth Unites “ The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics SIGN UP for my newsletter, Unseen Things . articles.title: I Was a Justice Warrior. I Needed the Whole Gospel. You Do Too.
articles.summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
articles.summary_zh: 从2016年到2018年,我是一个社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在Facebook和Twitter上, 如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到我在郊区一个保守的基督教家庭长大,或者我从4岁开始每天在基督教学校接受教育。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度.
articles.title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
articles.content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). This gospel of the kingdom must be lived out through embodied action. Mapping Our Approaches to Cross and Kingdom Most Christians today rightly see these two gospel aspects—the message proper and its kingdom implications—as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. As a result, many emphasize only one aspect or the other. And sadly, some neglect both these aspects of the gospel altogether. Nicholas Wolterstorff writes that shalom is “a harmony and delight in all of one’s relationships: between us and God, us and other people, us and other cultures, us and creation, and between us and our very selves.” In the four-quadrant grid below, I’ve mapped out the ways we typically approach the cross and kingdom aspects of the gospel. (For more, see section II.3 of The Gospel Coalition’s Theological Vision for Ministry .) Christ’s sacrifice on the cross restores us to harmony and delight with God. This is our most important relationship, and it’s represented on the diagram by the upward-pointing vertical axis. A kingdom emphasis on harmony and delight in other people, other cultures, and the creation is represented by the rightward-pointing horizontal axis. Quadrants II and IV represent two errors—the false choice of emphasizing either the cross or kingdom while neglecting the other. Many American Christians have been ensnared by one of these two quadrants. Quadrant III designates a total neglect of both cross and also kingdom. All these disconnects result from misunderstanding who a Christian is and what a Christian should do in this broken world. Quadrant IV: Individualized Gospel Advocates of an individualized gospel (quadrant IV) want to get people saved for the afterlife without stressing the social implications for this life. When sinners are saved, we always celebrate! However, Christians who fit in this quadrant often don’t emphasize the kingdom aspect of the gospel. Such individuals and churches may financially support ministries in underresourced neighborhoods but don’t often emphasize transformative service there. Many such churches and their members may not understand or appreciate the depth and range of problems in struggling communities, even in neighborhoods not far from them. Quadrant II: Social Gospel Advocates of the social gospel seek to meet people’s imminent needs but neglect their ultimate need of the salvation Jesus offers. This is a scandalous compromise, and it’s the false gospel I believed for nearly a decade and then proclaimed as a social media justice warrior. My wife and I moved into our underresourced neighborhood to live close to the school where I served for 18 years. Living and working among the poor showed me that many people need more than hearing about Jesus alone. They needed tangible help. Many of my quadrant IV friends concluded my neighbors were ignorant, dangerous, and to be avoided. So I reacted to my peers by propelling myself into the social gospel. Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. The social gospel is an late 19th- and early 20th-century theological movement focused on breaking the chains of oppression and championing the poor. Advocates seek to make Christ’s kingdom manifest on earth through acts of charity, philanthropy, and just legislation. Some social-gospel advocates choose to live close to the poor to improve their neighborhoods and lives. Yet the social gospel focuses solely on meeting imminent needs. It neglects preaching Christ as the sinner’s Savior. In fact, many social-gospel advocates reject the evangelical gospel and biblical authority. Many parachurch organizations that serve underresourced communities are held hostage by social-gospel theology. Though the leaders may be Christians, you can scour the organizations’ websites and messaging yet find no evidence of an orthodox theological foundation. Quadrant III: Faux Gospel Those who ignore both the gospel of the cross and the gospel of th

从2016年到2018年,我是一个社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在Facebook和Twitter上,
如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到我在郊区一个保守的基督教家庭长大,或者我从4岁开始每天在基督教学校接受教育。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度. 我把自己的生命交给了耶稣,我得知耶稣是来寻求拯救失落者.
然而,我青年中以福音为取向的世界被故意洗涤,并在10分钟后脱离了贫穷和不公正的痛苦现实。 当我发现这种差距,我成为在线上的正义战士。 虽然这种姿态无疑是对我成长的反应, 我的社交媒体宣传反映了我的真实生活.
我从2001年起就住在资源不足的街区工作。 在附近15年里, 我对邻居每天面临的状况 和美国教会中有多少人的生活脱节感到负担沉重。 我的教会生活和邻居之间的政治、种族和社会经济鸿沟使我心碎。
所以当我上网时,我确信我分享了真正的福音。 然而,我所分享的“神灵”仅仅集中于在这里和现在产生实际结果,而不是影响永恒。 我所需要的是一个整体的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕他为十字架上罪人而牺牲的死亡。
我开始在圣经福音书中看到两个方面。 让我们把他们称为十字架和王国的福音。 十字架的福音是好消息,耶稣基督通过他的替代死亡和光荣的复活来拯救并接纳信徒作为他的孩子. 我们天生都与上帝隔绝。 我们是他的敌人,
在基督中,我们相信好消息,因此与上帝和解(5:6-10),并与他保证永生(John 3:16). 正如彼得所写道的,“耶稣也曾因罪孽而受苦;正义者为不义之人所受苦,以便他能把我们带到上帝面前”(第3:18页)。
此外,《福音》的交叉方面强调,受委托传达这一信息的人必须与一个迷失和垂死的世界分享(Matt:28:18-20)。 十字架的福音必须预告;必须宣布。 这是优先事项。 从这个福音流出每一个好礼物。
我所需要的是一个整体的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕他为十字架上罪人而牺牲的死亡。 王国的福音是好消息,上帝的正义、善良与和平的意志已经释放出来。 作为上帝的子孙,信徒们被邀请参与见证王国使命的到来.
耶稣在部里首先发出一个信息,宣称“向穷人提供好消息”和“向被压迫者提供自由”(公爵4:18)。 他呼吁他的听众悔过自新, 他特别斥责法利赛人忽视“较重的法律问题:正义和仁慈以及忠诚”(23:23)。
保罗也教导道,福音不仅使我们与上帝团聚,而且通过在教会中调和分裂的人民来伸张正义。 他写道,“[基督]自己是我们的和平,他使我们两个[种族群 都成为和平,并用他的身体打破了敌对的分道扬镳”(第2:14页)。
我们遵守法律,通过我们作为立法者的身份,活出福音的王国意义(马特:9)。 福音的王国方面为我们提供了追求上帝 " 在地上像在天上一样 " 的旨意的愿景(6:10),即看到万事皆新(Rev.21:5). 这个王国的福音 必须通过体现的行动来活下来
今天,大多数基督徒正确地将这两个福音方面——信息本身及其王国影响——视为同一圣经派的一部分。 但我们往往不认为它们必然相互交织。 因此,许多人只强调某一个方面。 不幸的是,有些人完全忽略了福音的这两个方面。
尼古拉斯·沃尔特斯托夫(Nicholas Wolterstorff)写道:"在一个人的所有关系中,我们与上帝、我们与其他人、我们与其他文化、我们与创造之间,以及我们与我们自身之间,都是和谐和愉快的"。 在下面的四平地网格中, 我绘制了我们一般处理福音的十字和王国方面的方式。
(详见福音书联盟对部的神学观第二.3节. 基督在十字架上所做出的牺牲,使我们恢复了与上帝的和谐和喜悦。 这就是我们最重要的关系,它用向上指向的垂直轴来代表。
一个王国在其他人,其他文化中强调和谐与快乐,而创造者则以右向的横向轴为代表. 四方二和四代表两个错误——错误的选择是强调十字或王国,而忽略另一个。 许多美国基督徒被这两个四重奏之一所迷惑.
四方三指完全忽视了十字和王国. 所有这些脱节都是由于误解基督徒是谁,基督徒在这个破碎的世界中应该做什么. 四方四:一个个性化福音(quadrant IV)的个性化福音倡导者希望让人们为来世而得到救赎,而不要强调对这一生活的社会影响.
罪人获救后,我们总是庆祝! 基督教徒通常不强调福音的王国方面。 这些个人和教会可能会在资金不足的街区资助各部,
许多这类教会及其成员可能不了解或不明白在艰难的社区中,甚至在离他们不远的街区中,问题的严重性和范围。 四方二:社会福音 社会福音的倡导者试图满足人们的迫切需要,但却忽视他们对耶稣所提供的救赎的最终需要。
这也是我近十年来所相信的虚假福音, 我妻子和我搬到我们资源不足的街区 住在我工作了18年的学校附近 穷人中的生活和工作表明,许多人需要的不只是听到耶稣的孤独. 他们需要切实的帮助。
我的许多四分卫朋友都认为我的邻居是无知的,危险的,需要避免. 所以我对同伴们的反应是 推动自己进入社会福音。 今天大多数基督徒将这两个福音部分视为同为圣经派的一部分. 但我们往往不认为它们必然相互交织。
社会福音是19世纪后期和20世纪前期的神学运动,以打破被压迫的枷锁并拥护穷人为主. 通过慈善、慈善和公正立法, 一些社会神道的倡导者选择住在与穷人相近的地方来改善他们的邻居和生活.
然而,社会福音完全侧重于满足紧迫的需要。 它忽略了宣扬基督是罪人救世主. 事实上,许多社会-神道倡导者拒绝福音和圣经权威. 许多为资源不足的社区服务的教会组织被社会神学所牵制.
尽管领导者可能是基督徒,但你们可以搜索各组织的网站和消息,但却找不到正统神学基础的证据。 四方三:福州福音 那些无视十字架福音和福音的人

articles.title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
articles.summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
articles.summary_zh: “我从未担心过像希特勒这样的人。 ” 这不是一个疯子或有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些是一位牧师的话,他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁,他穿上了神的全盔并准备出战。 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰;
articles.title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
articles.content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. Throughout the church’s history, we’ve often turned to national politics. In a talk titled “ Living in Revolutionary Times ,” Lloyd-Jones rebukes the evangelicals of his day, who “seem to think that they are innovators in saying that we should all be taking an interest in politics and social matters.” But this is nothing new. Lloyd-Jones recalls, “They do not seem to have heard of the ‘social gospel’ craze of the earlier part of this century. All this has been tried with great thoroughness.” A preacher unaware of the dangerous pitfalls the church has already fallen into is sure to lead his congregation into one of those pits. This was the great danger, in Lloyd-Jones’s mind, of harnessing power for the church through political means. Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In that same talk, Lloyd-Jones cautions preachers against the temptation to quickly gather a crowd by preaching politics. His words feel even more timely today: I well remember certain men who were concerned about social and political matters, and who constantly preached on such themes, and packed their chapels for a while, but only as long as they preached politics. The moment they began to preach the gospel truly the crowds left them. Politically-minded people are always ready to make use of the church, but they always abandon and shun her when she ceases to be of any value to them. American pulpits have been infected with this kind of partisan preaching for decades now, on both the left and right. It draws crowds but does a disservice to the gospel. It’s important for Christians to offer a robust political and social ethic, but not at the expense of the gospel. The former flows from the latter, and the order is irreversible. Remember the ‘Leaven’ For Lloyd-Jones, spiritual resurrection—not political revolution—would save the world. The church didn’t need a theology of liberation but a theology of “leaven.” Drawing a straight line through the New Testament, he says , “The Christian is represented as ‘salt’ in society and ‘leaven,’ and surely the whole point of those comparisons is that Christian influence is to be a quiet influence and a slow process of influencing society.” Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In times of political crisis, such as our own, we’re tempted to forget this basic biblical principle. We must remember that “the kingdom of God is like leaven” (Matt. 13:33). If we’re to have social and political influence, it’ll only happen through preaching and preserving the gospel, so that regenerate Christians can be salt and light in the public square. On May 21, 1943, when Westminster Chapel was finally seeing signs of stability after the bombings, Lloyd-Jones wrote a letter responding to a congregant who was thanking him for his faithful preaching. He ended by saying , “The supreme need of the hour is intense prayer for spiritual revival on the part of Christian people.” The Doctor was interested in treating the disease, not the symptoms. That’s why he could speak with such audacity, testifying that he was “never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” As wicked as Hitler was, he was merely symptomatic of the spiritual disease of the human heart—to which the gospel alone is the cure.
articles.content_zh:
“我从未担心过像希特勒这样的人。” 这不是一个疯子或有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些是一位牧师的话,他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁,他穿上了神的全盔并准备出战。 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰;
第二天,马丁·劳埃德-琼斯 在伦敦的威斯敏斯特礼拜堂 担任助理牧师 他将在接下来的30年里 忠实地传教 传教士取道后一年,希特勒开始对伦敦的轰炸战役. 在该地区大约700所教堂中,有624所被炸毁,91所被完全摧毁。
令许多威斯敏斯特礼拜堂(Westminster Chapel)惊讶的是, Iain Murray在他的关于劳埃德-琼斯的经典传记中写道,
炸弹震动了整个建筑,石膏和灰尘落在会众上,包括劳埃德-琼斯所闻的“医生”上。 在暂停后,劳埃德-琼斯只是继续了他的祈祷,礼拜无阻地向前. Lloyd -Jones为我们的政治焦虑时期提供了必要的纠正。 一些基督徒诉诸于绝望,而另一些人则试图革命.
我们需要的是政治神学,当炸弹爆炸时,它仍然宣扬基督。 在政治危机时期, 我们可以从劳埃德-琼斯的部里学到三个教训。 当英格兰显然正在进入战争时,劳埃德-琼斯将他的妻子和他们的两个孩子送回威尔士并远离了这座城市,却不知道会发生什么事。
在一封与他妻子的简短而紧急的信件中,他写道:"也离开你和我,以及上帝手中的一切,你会得到平和与安息". 随着炸弹高空飞来,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷. 随着炸弹高空飞来,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷.
由于恐惧和恐慌,许多人开始放弃教会的武器,取而代之的是国家的武器. 但劳埃德-琼斯拒绝模糊界限.
当战争处于最坏的状态,由于死亡和流离失所,他的会众减少到很少的时候,他仍然坚决申明2个科林斯人10:4:“我们的战争武器不是同性相通的,而是通过上帝而强大的力量来拉倒坚固的阵地”(KJV)。
劳埃德-琼斯拒绝允许革命联盟和战术渗透到教会中去: 唉,教会经常试图用类似武器来对付被敌人所雇佣的人来对付世界及其迫害的力量. 她与国家结盟,并试图在物质意义上加强自己。
她一直缓慢地发现大卫很久以前在与高丽的战斗中发现的东西,即她不能在索尔的盔甲上出战,而必须永远使用她熟悉并打算使用的武器.
劳埃德-琼斯在索尔的军械库里看到类似的情况, 与大卫的悲哀一样,祈祷可能出现在世界的眼中,令人悲哀的是,反对法西斯主义的武器不足。 但上帝的武器比人的武器还多
反对党的福音 劳埃德-琼斯看到,当恐惧笼罩人民时,教会特别容易受到政治偶像崇拜的影响。 像在高丽之光下摇晃的以色列人一样,我们常常感到唯一的合理反应是找到我们自己的“强人”来战斗。 我们经常转向国家政治。
在一篇题为“生活在革命时报”的演讲中,劳埃德-琼斯斥责了当时的福音派,他们“似乎认为他们是创新者,认为我们大家都应该关心政治和社会事务。 但这不是什么新鲜事。 劳埃德-琼斯回忆说, " 他们似乎没有听说过本世纪上半叶的 " 社会福音 " 狂热。
所有这一切都经过了非常彻底的尝试。” 一个牧师不知道教堂已经陷入了危险的陷阱 肯定会把他的会众带到其中的一个坑里 在劳埃德-琼斯的心目中,这是通过政治手段掌握教会权力的巨大危险。
任何关于教会内部政治革命的言论, 在同一话中,劳埃德-琼斯告诫道教士不要通过宣扬政治来迅速聚集一众的诱惑.
他的话今天感觉更加及时:我清楚地记得某些关心社会和政治事务的人,他们不断地宣扬这些主题,打包他们的礼拜堂一段时间,但只要他们宣扬政治. 当他们开始宣扬福音时, 群众真的离开了他们。
有政治思想的人总是准备利用教堂,但当她不再对他们有任何价值时,他们总是抛弃并避开她. 美国的纸币 已经感染这种 党派传道 几十年了,左右两侧。 它吸引了人群,但不利于福音。
基督徒必须提供强有力的政治和社会道德, 前者从后者而来,而顺序是不可逆转的. 记住劳埃德-琼斯的"离开"(Leaven for Lloyd-Jones),精神复活——而不是政治革命——将拯救世界.
教会并不需要解放神学, 在新约中画出一条直线,他说 : “ 基督徒在社会中被代表为`盐'和`离开',这些比较的全部要点无疑是,基督教的影响是一种静默的影响,是影响社会的缓慢过程。 ” 任何关于教会内部政治革命的言论...
或号召基督教化国家, 在政治危机时期,比如我们自己的时代,我们想忘记这个基本的圣经原则。 我们必须记住,“上帝的王国就像一去不复返”(Matt. 13:33)。
我们只有通过传道和维护福音, 才能产生社会和政治影响, 1943年5月21日,当威斯敏斯特礼拜堂终于在轰炸后看到稳定的迹象时,劳埃德-琼斯写了一封信,答复了一位正在感谢他忠实地传道的教友.
他最后说,“最需要的是基督教人民强烈地祈祷精神复兴。” 医生对治疗疾病感兴趣,而不是症状。
因此,他可以如此大胆地说话,证明他“从来不担心像希特勒这样的人。 ” 与希特勒一样邪恶,他只是人类心灵的精神疾病的症状——只有福音才能治愈。

articles.title: Building a Workplace Where People Flourish (with Landon Hobson)
articles.summary: What happens when a seminary-trained economist takes over a pet-products plant? Landon Hobson, CEO of Cosmos Corporation, shares how paid mission days, a book club, and a ‘make the coffee’ ethic help ordinary workers flourish.
articles.summary_zh: 兰登·霍布森(Landon Hobson)是Cosmos Corporation的首席执行官,是圣路易斯外的一个家族企业,在70个国家销售宠物护理和家用清洁产品. 由于神学和经济学的学位,兰登从未预期会经营25万平方英尺的制造厂——直到他岳父要求他接管公司,他觉得上帝一直在为他做好确切的准备. Landon描述了他的信仰如何塑造Cosmos的文化:为雇员想要追求的任何学位提供学费支持,一个支付人们阅读费的"更好的书会",一年有5个付薪的任务日,以及为背后的人“愿意做咖啡”的核心价值. 他直言不讳地说, 连锁供应中断、销售量下降, 以及他所关心的人被解雇。
articles.title_zh: 打造让人们茁壮成长的工作场所（与Landon Hobson一起）
articles.content: Landon Hobson is the CEO of Cosmos Corporation, a family business outside St. Louis that makes pet care and household cleaning products sold in 70 countries. With degrees in theology and economics, Landon never expected to run a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant—until his father-in-law asked him to take over the company, and he sensed that God had been preparing him for exactly that. Landon describes how his faith shapes Cosmos’s culture: tuition support for any degree an employee wants to pursue, a “Better Book Club” that pays people to read, five paid mission days a year, and a core value of being “willing to make the coffee” for the person behind you. He answers hard questions about whether making dog shampoo really matters to God, and he speaks candidly about the hard years—supply chain disruptions, a drop in sales, and layoffs of people he cared about. He also explains why CEOs need pastors who aren’t passive, and what he has gained from a group of believing business leaders who share the same struggles. Resources Mentioned: To Change the World by James Davison Hunter Every Good Endeavor by Timothy Keller A Public Faith by Miroslav Volf Work in the Spirit by Miroslav Volf

articles.title: The Missing Piece in John Mark Comer’s Quiet Time
articles.summary: ‘Into the Quiet’ effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture.
articles.summary_zh: 根据近期的皮尤研究研究,超过半数的美国成年人报告说在智能手机上花费了太多的时间. 即使是那些承认智能手机上瘾负面影响的人,也觉得很难削减。 过度的屏幕时间不仅会损害我们的生产力和与其他人的联系,而且还会使修行精神学科更具挑战性。 John Mark Comer在其最新一书《静默:在噪音的世界中追随耶稣》中认为,“折磨一种孤独、沉默和静静的习俗对于繁荣的精神生活是绝对不可或缺的”(26)。
articles.title_zh: 约翰·马克·科默安静时光中缺失的部分
articles.content: According to a recent Pew Research study, more than half of U.S. adults report spending too much time on their smartphones. Even those who acknowledge the negative effects of smartphone addiction find it incredibly difficult to cut back. Excessive screen time isn’t just harming our productivity and connection with other people; it also makes practicing spiritual disciplines more challenging. In his latest book, Into the Quiet: Following Jesus in a World of Noise , John Mark Comer argues that “nurturing a practice of solitude, silence, and stillness is utterly indispensable to a flourishing spiritual life” (26). This timely book addresses important issues in a lively, engaging, and accessible manner. And though the staccato prose style sometimes borders on gimmicky, it’s never dull. Comer dons three hats, appearing as technoskeptic, therapist, and mystic. I responded differently to each: cheering the first, querying the second, and rejecting the third. Into the Quiet effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also makes questionable claims about the spiritual value of silence and promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture. Comer as Technoskeptic Comer’s consistent message is that readers need to intentionally disconnect from an increasingly noisy world. By “noise,” he means both literal sounds and the ever-present flood of distraction enabled by digital devices. The result is that “it is now possible to go through our entire lives and never be alone ” (18, emphasis original). Channeling secular authors like Jonathan Haidt and Johann Hari, Comer argues that constant noise threatens our well-being, whether we’re religious or not. But this dynamic is especially harmful for Christians. “Are we really surprised that . . . when we sit down to pray, we can barely even pay attention?” he asks (20). Our always-on lives differ greatly from the example of Jesus, who models a strategy of “retreat and return” (30). He ministers to the crowds and then withdraws to solitary places to pray (e.g., Matt. 14:23). This is the book’s strongest material, a timely warning with which I wholeheartedly agree. Comer as Therapist But then Comer moves in another direction. He advances therapeutic claims that may be helpful to some people but that aren’t clearly grounded in Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose: All of this stuff is in you . . . leaking out like toxic pollution into the water supply of your relational world . . . it’s asking to be dealt with. To be given a moment to speak, say its piece. To be healed. Released. (85) While the imprecatory psalms and the psalms of lament certainly model honest prayer before the Lord, and self-examination is clearly a biblical imperative, Comer’s specific claims seem more informed by extrabiblical therapeutic practices than by Scripture itself. Is it actually true that “naming our feelings out loud allows our bodies to process and discharge pain without it getting lodged in our cores” (100)? That doesn’t sound like Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose. The primary biblical support he gives for the practice of naming feelings to discharge pain is Jesus’s prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, an incident that provides the “template” for “the moments of our own Golgothas” (101). The problem is that Jesus in the garden isn’t surfacing old “toxic pollution” from “the water supply of [his] relational world” with an eye toward therapeutic healing (85). He’s facing an imminent crisis and asking the Father for either deliverance from or strength to face the trial set before him. Whatever the value of surfacing past trauma, Gethsemane doesn’t establish Comer’s claims on that point. Comer as Mystic It will be unsurprising for those who have followed Comer’s work, but he also emphasizes a form of mysticism that seeks direct, unmediated contact with God. This mysticism is an “aspect of our inner life” that is “a line of poetry from God . . . words fail here.” He concludes, “All I know is, when we sink down below the surface of all our busy, noisy, anxious minds, there is a vast ocean of peace deep inside . . . Oneing God” (194). For Comer, this intense spiritual experience can be equated with the Reformed doctrine of union with Christ. He argues, “Reformed Protestants use totally different language for a remarkably similar idea; they laud the joy of ‘union with Christ’” (192). Though it has experiential aspects and is sometimes referred to as “mystical union,” in Reformed theology “union with Christ” refers, in the first instance, to the objective work of the Holy Spirit through which a person is joined to Christ through faith and receives all his benefits thereby. It’s not a Reformed shorthand for a heightened, subjective, mystical experience that comes and goes. Though Comer identifies as a Protestant, he relies on numerous quotations from “desert fathers and mothers,” medieval mystics, and modern Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox theologians to justify his cafeteria approach to spirituality . As in his previous work, he engages with few heirs of the Reformation. Comer insists that Scripture is essential, but, for him, it doesn’t stand alone. Consistent with this non-Protestant mystical tradition, the book strongly emphasizes subjective, immediate communication from God apart from God’s inspired words in Scripture. He writes, “While Scripture is arguably the most important, and certainly the most authoritative way, we hear God’s voice, it’s not the only one” (180). In addition to the Bible, Comer stresses that we should “listen to the thoughts that come into our minds from God himself” (182). These messages arrive as the “faint whisper in the silence of our hearts,” and Comer claims that “hearing God’s voice” in this way is “just like learning to recognize any other voice” (183). Comer insists that Scripture is essential, but, for him, it doesn’t stand alone. Beyond asking whether a theological claim explicitly contradicts Scripture, we should also ask whether the Bible positively teaches it. Here’s where Comer’s presentation breaks down. Though Comer highlights mystical theologians who support his perspective, little biblical evidence supports the notion that one should, as a regular, ordinary part of the Christian life, expect God to speak apart from Scripture. Comer cites Elijah hearing the “still small voice” of God (1 Kings 19:12, KJV) and Jesus’s statement that “[his] sheep hear [his] voice” (John 10:27). Yet he provides no biblical argument for why God’s miraculous dealings with an Old Testament prophet should be taken as normative today, nor does he explain how the context of John 10 supports the idea that Jesus is referring there to the sort of “hearing” that Comer has in mind. Sola Scriptura or Silence? Untethering communication with God from Scripture often allows people to move in unhelpful and potentially spiritually dangerous directions. According to Comer, in addition to knowing God through his word, “there are aspects of God that you can experience only in the quiet” (173). If Comer simply means that we must shut out noisy distraction to truly focus on biblical truth then there would be no problem. But he seems to be saying something more. While it is not always entirely clear what Comer believes will happen in the quiet, he seems to teach that direct divine encounter through silence provides a second and separate path to knowing God. “We enter the quiet to search for God himself. To encounter him , to hear his voice, and to know his love” (172). I understand him to mean that this divine encounter and voice are distinct from and in addition to what we would get from Scripture alone. In this connection, he quotes Counter-Reformation mystic Teresa of Ávila (1515-1582) approvingly: “‘Settle yourself in solit

John Mark Comer在其最新一书《静默:在噪音的世界中追随耶稣》中认为,“折磨一种孤独、沉默和静静的习俗对于繁荣的精神生活是绝对不可或缺的”(26)。 这本及时的书以生动活泼、参与和无障碍的方式处理了重要问题。 虽然这种花花公子的花花样有时与花花公子相接,
来者会戴三顶帽子,以技术怀疑者、治疗师和神秘主义者的身份出现。 我对每一个都作出了不同的反应:欢呼第一个,询问第二个,拒绝第三个.
静悄悄地有效地批评了我们繁忙的文化时刻的弊端,但同时也对静悄悄的精神价值提出了有疑问的主张并宣扬了一种精神,这种精神可能很快地与"圣经"脱节. 读者需要有意与越来越吵的世界断绝联系。
他的“噪音”既指文字上的声音,又指数字设备所促成的无所不在的分心。 其结果是,“现在可以度过我们的整个生活,永远不要孤独......”(18,强调原文)。 Comer指出, 不断的噪音威胁着我们的福祉, 无论我们是否信奉宗教。
但这种动态对基督徒特别有害. “当我们坐下来祷告时,我们甚至几乎不能注意,我们真的感到惊讶吗?” 我们始终不渝地生活与耶稣的榜样大相径庭,耶稣仿效了“遣返和返回”(30)。 他的大臣们到人群中去,然后撤到单独的地方去祈祷(如Matt. 14:23).
这是这本书最强的材料, 来者是治疗师 但后来来者向另一个方向移动。 他提出治疗性主张,
据Comer说,孤独迫使与痛苦相对抗,这为基本的心理目的服务: 所有这些东西都在你体内... ...像有毒的污染一样 渗出到你的亲缘世界的供水中... 被给予发言的时间,说出它的一部分。 为被治. 释出.
(85) 虽然圣诗和哀叹的圣诗无疑是上帝面前的模范诚实祷告,而且自我检查显然是圣经的必经之事,但比起《圣经》本身,科默尔的具体说法似乎更能从圣经外的治疗做法中得到启发。
事实上,“大声点出我们的感情,让我们的身体能够处理并释放痛苦,而不将痛苦塞入我们的核心”(100)。 这听起来不像是圣经。 据Comer说,孤独迫使一种与痛苦相会的对抗,这种对抗服务于基本的心理目的.
耶稣在Gethsemane的花园里祈祷, 这是为“我们自己的Golgothas(101)时刻”提供“时代”的主要圣经支持。 问题是,花园里的耶稣并没有从“关系世界的供水”中冒出老“有毒污染”并着眼于治疗治疗(85)。
他正面临迫在眉睫的危机, Gethsemane并没有证明Comer对此的主张。
来者如神秘 追随Comer作品的人不会感到惊讶,但他也强调一种寻求与上帝直接,无媒介接触的神秘主义形式. 这种神秘主义是“我们内心生活的一面”,是“上帝的一行诗......。
这里的言辞失败了。” 他最后说,“我所知道的是,当我们沉入我们所有忙碌、吵闹和焦急的头脑的地表之下时,内心深处是一片巨大的和平之海......一个上帝”(194年)。 对于科默来说,这种强烈的精神经历可以等同于改革后与基督结合的学说. 他认为,“改革后的新教徒使用完全不同的语言来表达一种非常相似的想法;
他们赞扬 " 与基督结合 " (192)的喜悦。 虽然它具有经验性,有时被称为“神秘结合”,但在改革后神学“与基督结合”中,它首先是指圣灵的客观工作,通过这种工作,一个人通过信仰与基督结合,从而获得他的所有利益。
这并非一个经过改革的简写, 虽然科默尔将自己认定为新教徒,但他依靠许多来自“沙漠之父和母亲”中世纪神秘论和现代罗马天主教和东方东正教神学家的引文来证明他对精神的食堂方法是正确的。
和他之前的作品一样,他与改革派的少数继承人交往. 但对于他来说, 这并非孤立无援。 与这种非抗议的神秘传统相符合,这本书除了"圣经"中受上帝启发的话外,还极力强调主观的,与上帝的直接沟通.
他写道,"虽然圣经可以说是最重要的,当然也是最权威的方式,但我们听到的是上帝的声音,但这不是唯一的声音"(180). 除了"圣经",Comer强调,我们应当"倾听从上帝自己身上传入我们心中的思想"(182).
这些讯息是“在我们的心声中轻声低语”,而Comer声称,以这种方式“听到上帝的声音”“就像学会识别任何其他声音”(183)。 但对于他来说, 这并非孤立无援。
除了询问神学上的主张是否明确与"圣经"相矛盾外,我们还应该询问"圣经"是否正面地教导它. 以下为Comer的演讲内容。
虽然Comer强调支持他观点的神秘神学家,但鲜有圣经证据支持这样的观念,即一个人作为基督教生活中的常态,平凡的一部分,应该期待上帝能与"圣经"分开说话. Comer引述了以利亚听到上帝的"还很小的声音"(1 Kings 19:12, KJV)和耶稣的说法,即"他的羊听到他的声音"(John 10:27).
然而,他并没有提出圣经上的论点,说明为什么今天上帝与一位"旧约"先知的神奇交易应该被看作是规范的,他也没有解释约翰十世的背景如何支持耶稣在那里指的就是来宾所想的"听"那种"听"的想法. 索拉脚本还是沉默?
从"圣经"中脱去与上帝的沟通,往往可以使人们在无益和潜在的精神危险的方向上行走. 据Comer说,除了通过他的话来认识上帝之外,“上帝有些方面你只能在安静中经历”(173年)。
如果Comer只是意味着我们必须 避免吵闹的分心 真正专注于圣经的真理 那么就不会有问题了 但他似乎在说更多话 虽然并非总能完全清楚科默尔认为在静地中会发生什么,他似乎教导说,通过沉默直接的神通相会为了解上帝提供了第二条和单独的路径.
“我们进入静地去寻找上帝。 与他相会,听到他的声音,并了解他的爱"(172). 我理解他的意思是 这个神圣的相遇和声音 与我们单独从《圣经》中得到的东西不同 在这方面,他引用了Avila(1515-1582年)的反改革神秘特蕾莎的话说:“`将自己安置在单一的土地上。

articles.title: What Does It Mean to Be Human?: 12 Theses Answer a Pressing Question
articles.summary: Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good.
articles.summary_zh: 今天最有意义的是: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断上升,关于人性的辩论又再度出现. 文化现在似乎持有两种自相矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物, 或是我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 毫不奇怪,拒绝上帝会导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的混淆,认为我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,但作为创造之冠却有尊严。
articles.title_zh: 做人意味着什么？ ： 12篇论文回答了一个紧迫的问题
articles.content: No question today is more pertinent than this: What does it mean to be human? With declining belief in God and rising secularization come renewed debates concerning human nature. Culture now seems to hold to two contradictory beliefs: Either that we’re entirely material beings, meaningless clumps of matter in an endless void; or that we’re sovereign masters who determine our own meaning, with an internal sense of who we are that we dare not defy. It’s no surprise that rejections of God lead to confusion concerning the image of God and the biblical teaching that we’re humbly related to this material cosmos and yet dignified as the crown of creation. With the advent of artificial intelligence and ongoing debates about race, gender, and sexuality, it’s all the more important to be clear about what we are and who we’re made to be. Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. A Christian theological anthropology gets to the heart of who we are and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. In my book, For Us and for Our Salvation , I seek to address these issues by providing a biblical, theological, and practical introduction to the doctrines of humanity and sin. In this article, I present 12 theses that summarize a biblical and Reformed-catholic theological anthropology that I explain throughout the book. These 12 theses, I hope, can ground us as we stand in culture’s ever-changing landscape. 1. All human beings are made in the image of the triune God and are thus called to represent, enjoy, and glorify God forever. God creates each individual according to his image. The first-person plural in Genesis 1:26 indicates that the whole triune God is the archetype for the human being, for each person of the Trinity shares a singular divine substance (see also Col. 1:15–17). Humans are created as representatives of God and are thus religious creatures made to have communion with their Origin. Therefore, each human being as such is created good, with dignity and agency. Our religiosity, corrupted by the fall, doesn’t lead us to cease being religious but rather causes us to elevate and idolize one aspect of creation over others, as we prefer the creature over the Creator (Rom. 1:18–23). We refuse to acknowledge God as the end for which we were made, and we seek enjoyment in other things—we idolize good, created reality and render it ultimate. 2. The doctrine of the image of God entails both ontological and ethical affirmations. God creates humans as embodied souls with intellectual and volitional capacities, and he calls humans to represent him by a proper exercise of those faculties in righteousness, holiness, and true knowledge. Human beings are endowed with capacities for wisdom and righteousness. A twofold metaphysical concept is important here: act and potency. Potency refers to the natural power that distinguishes a particular kind of thing from other kinds, and act refers to the exercise of that power. Humans, for instance, are the kinds of beings endowed with the potency to think rationally, but the actualization of those potencies is a distinct matter. Edward Feser clarifies , In arguing for the existence of active potencies or causal powers, Scholastic writers emphasize the point that a cause is not always bringing about its characteristic effect. . . . My power to write must therefore be distinguished from this or that actual, particular action of writing, as a standing precondition of the latter. Infants or those in a comatose state due to some serious injury, therefore, continue to be image-bearers, even while the potency for wisdom or will isn’t actualized in any way. Similarly, those who are cognitively impaired still have the potency or essential capacity of reason and volition even though it manifests differently than in others, and even if the exercise of those powers is only actualized in the resurrection. (By contrast, a hypothetically resurrected squirrel will never actualize powers of rationality, because it was never in its nature to possess this capacity.) If humans are the particular creatures called to be in communion with and representatives of God, then such potencies are precisely those presupposed to make them fitting for the task. This focus on what human beings are , with its attendant formal capacities (or essential potencies), then, doesn’t introduce a gradation for the image of God but rather complements and grounds the emphasis on human dignity. Every human is made in the image of God, whether or not he or she actualizes wisdom or righteousness. 3. Just as the visible creation witnesses to the invisible God, the image of God includes the body, as shown in its created goodness, dependence, and fittingness for the soul. The body is a fitting home for the soul, and the soul is, in turn, the form of the body. As embodied souls, humans image God through their sexed bodies, and their personalities are communicated by way of embodiment. God has created our bodies good , has assumed one in the incarnation, and is committed to resurrect them in the consummation of the new creation. The body is thus a reminder of humanity’s humility and exaltation (Ps. 8). Humans represent God and yet absolutely depend on God. Humans are privileged to be embodied. Grasping our distinctiveness—even from that of the angels—can help us think well about artificial intelligence. Consider the parallels between angels and AI: Both are free from bodily limitations, both are said to be more intelligent than humans (although, angels also have a unique intelligence that AI cannot possess), both have longer lifespans, and both have access to a wealth of information that no human does. One might ask the question this way: If the angels were created a little higher than humanity (v. 5), why is it good for us , not them, to be the image and representation of God? The answer lies in our embodied agency and relational responsibilities toward one another. Wisdom and righteousness are embodied virtues. We bear unique responsibility for the other, as we share familial and natural relations with each other. Angels and AI cannot replicate this familial or physical bond and thus cannot participate in the care and love intrinsic to human relations and requisite for human wisdom and righteous love for God and neighbor. When a human is righteous or fails to be righteous, his community rises or falls with him. AI can neither take the blame nor be responsible for the well-being or demise of humanity; it cannot come alongside humanity and participate in its embodied experiences, suffering, or joy. The responsibility for AI is traceable back to its producers and users. Human embodiment isn’t a detrimental weakness of our nature that makes us inferior to the angels or AI, but it enriches human existence with a complex web of relations and a redemptive-history into which angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12) and about which silicon machines cannot know. 4. The image of God entails stewarding and cultivating creation: the cultural mandate. The cultural mandate is the vocational aspect of the image of God. God calls human beings to be fruitful and multiply (Gen. 1:28), and this involves not merely procreation but also the cultivation of creation through the formation of culture. If God creates out of nothing, humans create out of nature. Human embodiment isn’t a detrimental weakness of our nature that makes us inferior to the angels or AI. As human beings spread across the globe, so is the glory of God spreading through human representation. This natural development leads to the affirmation that cultural diversity itself is good. Given the fall, however, cultural diversity is mired in sin and leads to much conflict and division. This side of the fall, the cultural mandate is carried out not merely by the natur
articles.content_zh:
今天最有意义的是: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断上升,关于人性的辩论又再度出现. 文化现在似乎持有两种自相矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物,
或是我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 毫不奇怪,拒绝上帝会导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的混淆,认为我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,但作为创造之冠却有尊严。
随着人工智能的出现和关于种族,性别,和性问题的持续辩论,更需要弄清楚我们是什么人,我们是谁。 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术实践. 它触及我们是谁的核心, 解释我们的日常经历, 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。
一个基督教神学人类学 得到了我们的心脏 我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。 在我《为了我们和我们的救世主》一书中,我试图通过提供一本圣经、神学和关于人类和罪恶理论的实际介绍来解决这些问题。
在这篇文章中,我提出了12篇论文,总结了一本圣经和经过改革的天主教神学人类学,我在全书中都对此作了解释. 我希望这12篇论文能让我们在文化不断变化的地貌中立足。 1. 所有的人都是以三位一体的上帝为形象而成的,因此被召唤来代表、享受并永远地颂扬上帝。
上帝根据自己的形象创造每个人. Genesis 1:26中的第一人称复数表示,整个地心神是人类的原型,对于"三一"中的每个人来说,都有一个独有的神性物质(也见1:15-17). 人类是作为上帝的代表而被创造的,因此是宗教活生生的被赋予了同其起源的圣体.
因此,每个人都是善良的、有尊严和有作用的。 我们的信仰被堕落所腐蚀, 并不导致我们不再信奉宗教, 而是导致我们提升和崇拜创造的一面,
我们拒绝承认神是我们的最终目的,我们寻求享受其他事物——我们崇拜善良,创造现实,使它达到最终目的。 2. 关于上帝形象的理论包括本体论和伦理论。
上帝以智慧和意志能力创造出众生 以正义、圣洁和真实知识 来代表人类 人类拥有智慧和正义的能力。 这里有一个双重元概念:行为和力量。
可能(potency)指将某种特定事物区别于其他类型的自然力量,而行为则指行使这种力量. 例如,人类就是那些具有理性思考能力的生物,但是,这些能力的实现是一个独特的问题。
Edward Feser澄清说,在论证存在主动的力量或因果力量时,学术作家强调一个原因并不总是能产生其特征效应.  . 因此,必须区分我的写作能力与这一或这一实际的、特别的写作行动,作为后者的长期先决条件。
婴儿或因严重伤害而处于昏迷状态的婴儿,
同样,那些在认知上受损的人仍然具有理智和意志的能力或基本能力,尽管这种能力的表现与其他人不同,即使行使这些权力只是在复活时才得到实现。
(相比之下,假想复活的松鼠永远不会实现理性的力量,因为拥有这种能力在性质上从来没有. ) 如果人类是被召来与上帝和上帝代表共同生活的特殊生物,那么这种力量正是预先假定的,使之适合这项任务。
关注人类的本质, 及其相应的正式能力(或基本力量), 每个人类都是以上帝的形象来塑造的,无论他是否实现智慧或正义. 3个
正如可见的创造物见证了无形的上帝一样,上帝的形象包括了身体,这表现在它创造的善良,依赖,和对灵魂的适应性上. 身体是灵魂的相宜之地,而灵魂又反过来成为了身体的形态. 作为被所象征的灵魂,人类通过被性别化的身体来形象地塑造出上帝,他们的个性通过被化为化身的方式来沟通.
上帝创造了我们的身体, 假设一个在化身中, 并致力于将它们复活 在新创造的集合。 因此,该机构提醒人们注意人类的谦卑和赞美(临8)。 人类代表着上帝,但绝对依赖于上帝。 人类享有被体现的特权。
我们的特异性——即使是天使的特异性——能够帮助我们很好地思考人工智能。
想想天使和AI的相似之处:两者都不受身体限制,据说两者都比人类更聪明(尽管天使也拥有AI不能拥有的独特智能),两者寿命都更长,并且都能够获取人类没有的丰富信息.
人们可能会这样问:如果创造的天使比人类更高一点(v. 5),为什么做上帝的形象和代表对我们而不是他们有好处? 答案在于我们体现的机构以及彼此的关系责任。 智慧与正等正等正等正觉即是正等正觉.
我们对另一方负有独特的责任,因为我们彼此有家庭和自然的关系。 天使和AI不能复制这种家庭或肉体的纽带,因此不能参与人类关系所固有的、人类智慧和对上帝和邻居的正义爱所必须的关爱和爱。
当人有义有义,或失义有义,则同其群起或相倒. 大赦国际既不能承担罪责,也不能为人类的福祉或灭亡负责;它不能与人类并肩而来,参与其固有的经历、苦难或欢乐。 AI的责任可以追溯到它的生产者和使用者.
人类的化身并不是我们本性的一个有害的弱点, 它让我们比天使或AI更低等, 4. 神的形象包括管理和培育创造:文化使命。
文化使命是上帝形象的职业方面。 上帝称人类是有成果和有倍增的(Gen. 1:28),这不仅涉及生育,而且涉及通过形成文化来培育创造. 如果上帝无所事事地创造,人类则由自然而生.
人类的化身并不是我们本质的有害弱点, 随着人类在全球的传播,上帝的光荣也通过人类代表来传播。 这种自然发展导致确认文化多样性本身是好的。 然而,由于文化的衰落,文化多样性陷入了罪恶之中,导致许多冲突和分裂。
秋天的这一边 文化任务不仅仅是由天来完成
