featured.summary: Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good.
featured.summary_zh: 今天最有意义的是: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断上升,关于人性的辩论又再度出现. 文化现在似乎持有两种自相矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物, 或是我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 毫不奇怪,拒绝上帝会导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的混淆,认为我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,但作为创造之冠却有尊严。
featured.title_zh: 做人意味着什么？ ： 12篇论文回答了一个紧迫的问题
featured.content: No question today is more pertinent than this: What does it mean to be human? With declining belief in God and rising secularization come renewed debates concerning human nature. Culture now seems to hold to two contradictory beliefs: Either that we’re entirely material beings, meaningless clumps of matter in an endless void; or that we’re sovereign masters who determine our own meaning, with an internal sense of who we are that we dare not defy. It’s no surprise that rejections of God lead to confusion concerning the image of God and the biblical teaching that we’re humbly related to this material cosmos and yet dignified as the crown of creation. With the advent of artificial intelligence and ongoing debates about race, gender, and sexuality, it’s all the more important to be clear about what we are and who we’re made to be. Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. A Christian theological anthropology gets to the heart of who we are and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. In my book, For Us and for Our Salvation , I seek to address these issues by providing a biblical, theological, and practical introduction to the doctrines of humanity and sin. In this article, I present 12 theses that summarize a biblical and Reformed-catholic theological anthropology that I explain throughout the book. These 12 theses, I hope, can ground us as we stand in culture’s ever-changing landscape. 1. All human beings are made in the image of the triune God and are thus called to represent, enjoy, and glorify God forever. God creates each individual according to his image. The first-person plural in Genesis 1:26 indicates that the whole triune God is the archetype for the human being, for each person of the Trinity shares a singular divine substance (see also Col. 1:15–17). Humans are created as representatives of God and are thus religious creatures made to have communion with their Origin. Therefore, each human being as such is created good, with dignity and agency. Our religiosity, corrupted by the fall, doesn’t lead us to cease being religious but rather causes us to elevate and idolize one aspect of creation over others, as we prefer the creature over the Creator (Rom. 1:18–23). We refuse to acknowledge God as the end for which we were made, and we seek enjoyment in other things—we idolize good, created reality and render it ultimate. 2. The doctrine of the image of God entails both ontological and ethical affirmations. God creates humans as embodied souls with intellectual and volitional capacities, and he calls humans to represent him by a proper exercise of those faculties in righteousness, holiness, and true knowledge. Human beings are endowed with capacities for wisdom and righteousness. A twofold metaphysical concept is important here: act and potency. Potency refers to the natural power that distinguishes a particular kind of thing from other kinds, and act refers to the exercise of that power. Humans, for instance, are the kinds of beings endowed with the potency to think rationally, but the actualization of those potencies is a distinct matter. Edward Feser clarifies , In arguing for the existence of active potencies or causal powers, Scholastic writers emphasize the point that a cause is not always bringing about its characteristic effect. . . . My power to write must therefore be distinguished from this or that actual, particular action of writing, as a standing precondition of the latter. Infants or those in a comatose state due to some serious injury, therefore, continue to be image-bearers, even while the potency for wisdom or will isn’t actualized in any way. Similarly, those who are cognitively impaired still have the potency or essential capacity of reason and volition even though it manifests differently than in others, and even if the exercise of those powers is only actualized in the resurrection. (By contrast, a hypothetically resurrected squirrel will never actualize powers of rationality, because it was never in its nature to possess this capacity.) If humans are the particular creatures called to be in communion with and representatives of God, then such potencies are precisely those presupposed to make them fitting for the task. This focus on what human beings are , with its attendant formal capacities (or essential potencies), then, doesn’t introduce a gradation for the image of God but rather complements and grounds the emphasis on human dignity. Every human is made in the image of God, whether or not he or she actualizes wisdom or righteousness. 3. Just as the visible creation witnesses to the invisible God, the image of God includes the body, as shown in its created goodness, dependence, and fittingness for the soul. The body is a fitting home for the soul, and the soul is, in turn, the form of the body. As embodied souls, humans image God through their sexed bodies, and their personalities are communicated by way of embodiment. God has created our bodies good , has assumed one in the incarnation, and is committed to resurrect them in the consummation of the new creation. The body is thus a reminder of humanity’s humility and exaltation (Ps. 8). Humans represent God and yet absolutely depend on God. Humans are privileged to be embodied. Grasping our distinctiveness—even from that of the angels—can help us think well about artificial intelligence. Consider the parallels between angels and AI: Both are free from bodily limitations, both are said to be more intelligent than humans (although, angels also have a unique intelligence that AI cannot possess), both have longer lifespans, and both have access to a wealth of information that no human does. One might ask the question this way: If the angels were created a little higher than humanity (v. 5), why is it good for us , not them, to be the image and representation of God? The answer lies in our embodied agency and relational responsibilities toward one another. Wisdom and righteousness are embodied virtues. We bear unique responsibility for the other, as we share familial and natural relations with each other. Angels and AI cannot replicate this familial or physical bond and thus cannot participate in the care and love intrinsic to human relations and requisite for human wisdom and righteous love for God and neighbor. When a human is righteous or fails to be righteous, his community rises or falls with him. AI can neither take the blame nor be responsible for the well-being or demise of humanity; it cannot come alongside humanity and participate in its embodied experiences, suffering, or joy. The responsibility for AI is traceable back to its producers and users. Human embodiment isn’t a detrimental weakness of our nature that makes us inferior to the angels or AI, but it enriches human existence with a complex web of relations and a redemptive-history into which angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12) and about which silicon machines cannot know. 4. The image of God entails stewarding and cultivating creation: the cultural mandate. The cultural mandate is the vocational aspect of the image of God. God calls human beings to be fruitful and multiply (Gen. 1:28), and this involves not merely procreation but also the cultivation of creation through the formation of culture. If God creates out of nothing, humans create out of nature. Human embodiment isn’t a detrimental weakness of our nature that makes us inferior to the angels or AI. As human beings spread across the globe, so is the glory of God spreading through human representation. This natural development leads to the affirmation that cultural diversity itself is good. 今天最有意义的是: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断上升,关于人性的辩论又再度出现. 文化现在似乎持有两种自相矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物,
或是我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 毫不奇怪,拒绝上帝会导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的混淆,认为我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,但作为创造之冠却有尊严。
随着人工智能的出现和关于种族,性别,和性问题的持续辩论,更需要弄清楚我们是什么人,我们是谁。 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术实践. 它触及我们是谁的核心, 解释我们的日常经历, 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。
一个基督教神学人类学 得到了我们的心脏 我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。 在我《为了我们和我们的救世主》一书中,我试图通过提供一本圣经、神学和关于人类和罪恶理论的实际介绍来解决这些问题。
在这篇文章中,我提出了12篇论文,总结了一本圣经和经过改革的天主教神学人类学,我在全书中都对此作了解释. 我希望这12篇论文能让我们在文化不断变化的地貌中立足。 1. 所有的人都是以三位一体的上帝为形象而成的,因此被召唤来代表、享受并永远地颂扬上帝。
上帝根据自己的形象创造每个人. Genesis 1:26中的第一人称复数表示,整个地心神是人类的原型,对于"三一"中的每个人来说,都有一个独有的神性物质(也见1:15-17). 人类是作为上帝的代表而被创造的,因此是宗教活生生的被赋予了同其起源的圣体.
因此,每个人都是善良的、有尊严和有作用的。 我们的信仰被堕落所腐蚀, 并不导致我们不再信奉宗教, 而是导致我们提升和崇拜创造的一面,
我们拒绝承认神是我们的最终目的,我们寻求享受其他事物——我们崇拜善良,创造现实,使它达到最终目的。 2. 关于上帝形象的理论包括本体论和伦理论。
上帝以智慧和意志能力创造出众生 以正义、圣洁和真实知识 来代表人类 人类拥有智慧和正义的能力。 这里有一个双重元概念:行为和力量。
可能(potency)指将某种特定事物区别于其他类型的自然力量,而行为则指行使这种力量. 例如,人类就是那些具有理性思考能力的生物,但是,这些能力的实现是一个独特的问题。
Edward Feser澄清说,在论证存在主动的力量或因果力量时,学术作家强调一个原因并不总是能产生其特征效应.  . 因此,必须区分我的写作能力与这一或这一实际的、特别的写作行动,作为后者的长期先决条件。
婴儿或因严重伤害而处于昏迷状态的婴儿,
同样,那些在认知上受损的人仍然具有理智和意志的能力或基本能力,尽管这种能力的表现与其他人不同,即使行使这些权力只是在复活时才得到实现。
(相比之下,假想复活的松鼠永远不会实现理性的力量,因为拥有这种能力在性质上从来没有. ) 如果人类是被召来与上帝和上帝代表共同生活的特殊生物,那么这种力量正是预先假定的,使之适合这项任务。
关注人类的本质, 及其相应的正式能力(或基本力量), 每个人类都是以上帝的形象来塑造的,无论他是否实现智慧或正义. 3个
正如可见的创造物见证了无形的上帝一样,上帝的形象包括了身体,这表现在它创造的善良,依赖,和对灵魂的适应性上. 身体是灵魂的相宜之地,而灵魂又反过来成为了身体的形态. 作为被所象征的灵魂,人类通过被性别化的身体来形象地塑造出上帝,他们的个性通过被化为化身的方式来沟通.
上帝创造了我们的身体, 假设一个在化身中, 并致力于将它们复活 在新创造的集合。 因此,该机构提醒人们注意人类的谦卑和赞美(临8)。 人类代表着上帝,但绝对依赖于上帝。 人类享有被体现的特权。
我们的特异性——即使是天使的特异性——能够帮助我们很好地思考人工智能。
想想天使和AI的相似之处:两者都不受身体限制,据说两者都比人类更聪明(尽管天使也拥有AI不能拥有的独特智能),两者寿命都更长,并且都能够获取人类没有的丰富信息.
人们可能会这样问:如果创造的天使比人类更高一点(v. 5),为什么做上帝的形象和代表对我们而不是他们有好处? 答案在于我们体现的机构以及彼此的关系责任。 智慧与正等正等正等正觉即是正等正觉.
我们对另一方负有独特的责任,因为我们彼此有家庭和自然的关系。 天使和AI不能复制这种家庭或肉体的纽带,因此不能参与人类关系所固有的、人类智慧和对上帝和邻居的正义爱所必须的关爱和爱。
当人有义有义,或失义有义,则同其群起或相倒. 大赦国际既不能承担罪责,也不能为人类的福祉或灭亡负责;它不能与人类并肩而来,参与其固有的经历、苦难或欢乐。 AI的责任可以追溯到它的生产者和使用者.
人类的化身并不是我们本性的一个有害的弱点, 它让我们比天使或AI更低等, 4. 神的形象包括管理和培育创造:文化使命。
文化使命是上帝形象的职业方面。 上帝称人类是有成果和有倍增的(Gen. 1:28),这不仅涉及生育,而且涉及通过形成文化来培育创造. 如果上帝无所事事地创造,人类则由自然而生.
人类的化身并不是我们本质的有害弱点, 随着人类在全球的传播,上帝的光荣也通过人类代表来传播。 这种自然发展导致确认文化多样性本身是好的。 然而,由于文化的衰落,文化多样性陷入了罪恶之中,导致许多冲突和分裂。

featured.content: In a conversation at church one Sunday, a pastor told a friend of mine, “Your friend should quit trying to plant churches in the inner city. It doesn’t happen because it can’t happen.” I was visiting this friend just before COVID-19 hit, speaking at a separate church about our ministry, New England Urban Church Planting. Our organization was new, and my sinful inclination was to think, Oh, you just wait and see! My friend was equally defensive. Yet this pastor was onto something: It rarely happens, and it is indeed hard. Why is church planting in our nation’s neglected inner cities so rare? Why are underserved urban communities overlooked by gospel-preaching churches? Stakeholders in our ministry have discussed these questions since 2009, leading to the organization’s founding in 2020. We’ve learned a lot in these years of full-time work as we’re growing this network of inner-city planters. The work is hard for two key reasons. Yet it’s possible. And it’s crucial. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations (Matt. 28:19)—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries. Problem Unless you grew up in the inner city, serving there is a cross-cultural experience. This is the first reason church planting hard. Ruby Payne asks her readers if they can survive in poverty: Do you know how to keep your clothes from being stolen from a laundromat? Do you know how to move in half a day? Do you know how to keep your car from getting repossessed if you fall behind on payments? Discipling men and women in the inner city can be exasperating when they have a new burner phone frequently. Inner-city pastors need to know how to preach and how to administer Narcan. And behind all that is the sound of gunshots, fights, loud TVs, and the quiet exit of well-meaning suburban Christians who came to help but didn’t last long. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. Evangelicalism often feels like it’s married to only one culture: suburbia. Postwar Americans migrated from our cities to set up homes and churches in the suburbs. In 1940, 15 percent of Americans lived in the suburbs. By 2000, that number was 50 percent. Evangelicals were a disproportionately high percentage of those who made the move. As this happened, Brian Miller argues , the values of suburbia melded with and shaped the values of evangelicalism. Churches in impoverished neighborhoods are rarely financially self-sustaining—the second challenge. Even if a pastor disciples his church toward generosity, being generous with a poverty-level income won’t pay the bills. So pastors who serve in these places get beaten down by serving a needy congregation while holding two other jobs “on the side.” It’s unsustainable. We don’t believe the answer for inner-city pastors should be a bi- or trivocational life. Solution The solution to these two challenges is within reach: the model of a supported foreign missionary. Since the late 18th century, the church has been training and sustaining men and women for gospel work in unfamiliar places, where they cannot expect the financial support of locals. This training-and-supporting model should be applied to inner-city church planting. The change we need has four aspects. The first is a change of heart. We need gospel-saturated hearts that understand that all people are impoverished by sin. Those living in a homeless encampment share the same fundamental condition as the wealthy suburbanite. Filled with gospel grace, we can move toward the poor because we’re more alike at heart than we are different. Our hearts must be shaped by the reality of Christ’s initiative to leave the riches of heaven for us, to become poor for us, that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Second, we need to believe that God’s heart is particularly inclined toward the overlooked (Ps. 72:12–14) and toward those generous toward them (Prov. 14:21). Generosity should begin with planting churches; the greatest mercy we can bring to underserved communities is a healthy church. After all, Martin Luther said , “After the preaching of the gospel, the office and charge of a true and faithful pastor is to be mindful of the poor.” Let’s be mindful of the poor with the preaching of the gospel in the context of inner-city churches. Third, we need strategic minds to see that the American church can sustain inner-city churches just as we do global missionaries. It’s a foolish church that would send a missionary to unreached people groups with the promise of three years of step-down funding. Similarly, we shouldn’t send inner-city pastors and their staff members to their neighborhood with only short-term start-up money and the expectation that they’ll somehow figure out how to sustain the ministry. Fourth, we need to train inner-city missionaries. The unique subculture calls for dedicated training. Just as a newly graduated MD needs a residency in her specialty before she can practice, so seminary graduates need specialized training in urban anthropology, missiology, ecclesiology, apologetics, and preaching before planting and pastoring. They need a well-formed biblical understanding of the relationship between mercy ministry and gospel discipleship. They need to know how to handle gangs, dealers, the undocumented, and mental health challenges. All We Need If we believe the American church can’t plant healthy, Christ-exalting churches in the inner city, this will be unique in the history of modern missions. To my knowledge, the American church has never considered a people group to be beyond our reach. We mustn’t start now. Planters need to know how to handle gangs, dealers, the undocumented, and mental health challenges. We have much to gain in doing so. Foremost is the glory of Christ, whose name is to be known and worshiped everywhere. His glory alone is worth our effort. Second is the opportunity to tell of a Savior who proclaimed good news to the poor (Luke 4:18). That good news is Jesus himself, who paid the debt of sin for all people and fulfilled the promise of Isaiah: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you who have no money, come, buy and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost” (Isa. 55:1, NIV). Third, we gain God’s blessing. His heart is inclined toward the overlooked and toward those generous toward them. If we want to be blessed, we must care for the needy. We also face a great danger in not doing so. James links good deeds with genuine faith and warns that neglect of the needy is a sign of false faith: Suppose a brother or a sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and well fed,” but does nothing about their physical needs, what good is it? In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead. (James 2:15–17, NIV) Dead faith isn’t saving faith. Perhaps the greater danger is neglecting our inner cities, not walking down their sidewalks. The Great Commission includes our inner cities. Yet we’ve often neglected this work, believing there’s no model that allows us to plant churches in these communities. But there is. It’s the missionary model. We have all we need: a commission from Christ, the promise of his presence, the Holy Spirit, the Word of God, a clear need, and a tested model. It’s time we put that model to work here in our inner cities.

一名牧师在一个星期日在教堂的谈话中告诉我的朋友说,“你的朋友应该停止试图在内城种植教堂。 这不可能发生, 我在COVID-19袭击前拜访了这个朋友 在另外的教堂里 谈到我们的部,新英格兰城市教会计划
我们的组织是新的, 我罪恶的倾向是想, 哦,你等着瞧! 我的朋友同样是防御性的。 然而这位牧师却发现了一些事情: 它很少发生,而且确实很困难。 为什么我们国家被忽视的内地城市的教堂种植如此罕见? 为什么福音教堂忽略了服务不足的城市社区?
本部的利益攸关方自2009年起讨论这些问题, 这些年来,我们在全职工作上学到了很多东西, 因为我们正在培育这个城市内部种植者网络。 这项工作很艰苦,有两个关键原因。 然而, 这很重要。 基督命令我们造出所有国家的门徒(Matt.
28:19) - 这包括在我国的内地城市. 为了在这些空间里种下教堂,我们需要像传教士一样思考. 问题 除非你在城内长大 在那里服务有跨文化的经验 这是教会植入硬树的第一个原因. 鲁比 Payne问读者能否在贫困中活下来: 你知道如何防止衣服被洗衣店偷走吗?
你知道怎么在半天内搬家吗? 你知道如何防止你的车 被收回 如果你落在支付落后? 内城的散去男女在频繁地拥有一款新的燃烧器手机时会令人兴奋. 市内牧师需要知道如何传教,如何管理纳尔坎.
以及心怀善意的郊区基督徒静静地离开, 基督命令我们使所有国家的门徒 -- -- 包括我们国家内部的城市。 福音派常常觉得它只与一种文化成婚:郊区.
战后美国人从我们的城市迁移到郊区建立家园和教堂. 1940年,15%的美国人住在郊区. 到2000年,这一数字为50%。 福音派教徒在采取行动者中所占比例过高。 并塑造福音派的价值观。
贫困街区的教会很少在财政上能够自我维持,这是第二个挑战。 即使牧师门徒们慷慨解囊, 因此,在这些地方工作的牧师们在“边上”从事另外两项工作时,却因为需要帮助的会众服务而遭到殴打。 这是不可持续的。
我们不相信市内牧师的答案应该是双职业或三职业生活。 解决方案 解决这两项挑战的办法是可以做到的:一个得到支持的外国传教士的模式。 自18世纪后期起,教会开始对在不熟悉的地方从事福音工作的男女进行培训和维持,他们无法指望当地人给予财政支持.
这种培训和支助模式应适用于市内教堂的种植。 我们需要的变革有四个方面。 初一一一一一一一一变化相. 我们需要福音饱和的心 理解所有的人 都因罪恶而贫穷 生活在无家可归营地的人与富裕的郊区有着同样的基本条件。
因为我们内心更加相似, 我们的心必须被基督倡议的现实所塑造,即把天堂的财富留给我们,让我们变得贫穷,让我们变得富有(第8:9节)。 第二,我们需要相信上帝的心特别倾向于被忽视的人(P.
72:12-14),以及对那些对他们慷慨的人(14:21. 慷慨应该从种植教堂开始;我们能够给服务不足的社区带来的最大的怜悯是一座健康的教堂。
毕竟,马丁·路德说:“在福音传道之后,一个真正和忠实的牧师的办公室和职责是注意穷人。” 在城市内部的教会中, 第三,我们需要有战略头脑,看到美国教堂可以维持市内教堂,就像我们做全球传教士一样。
将派遣一名传教士前往未触及的民众团体, 我们不应该派市内牧师及其工作人员到他们的社区去, 第四,要培养城内传教士.
独特的亚文化需要专门的训练。 正如刚毕业的MD在执业前需要她专业的居住权,因此神学院毕业生需要在城市人类学,误学,生态学,杂技学,以及播种和牧师前传教的专业培训.
他们需要对慈悲部和福音门徒的关系有一个完善的圣经理解. 他们需要知道如何应对帮派、毒贩、无证和心理健康挑战。 我们需要的 如果我们相信美国教会不能在内城栽培健康而赞美基督的教堂,这将在现代传教史上是独一无二的.
据我所知,美国教会从未认为一个民族团体是我们无法达到的。 我们不应该从现在开始。 种植园主需要知道如何对付帮派、毒贩、无证和心理健康挑战。 我们这样做可获益匪浅。 最先是基督的荣耀,其名将出名并随地被崇拜. 他的光荣值得我们努力。
第二是向穷人宣布好消息的救世主的机会(公爵4:18)。 这个好消息是耶稣自己,他为世人偿还了罪恶之债,并且履行了以赛亚的诺言:"你们这些渴渴的人,都来吧!你们这些没钱的人,来买东西吃东西吧! 来来来来来来来来来来来来去去,不花钱买酒和牛奶”(Isa. 55:1, NIV.
第三,我们得到了上帝的祝福。 他的心倾向于被忽略的人和对他们慷慨的人。 如果我们想要得到祝福,我们必须照顾需要帮助的人。 如果不这样做,我们也面临极大的危险。 詹姆斯将善行与真诚的信念联系起来,并警告说,忽视需要帮助的人是一种虚假的信仰:假设兄弟或姐妹没有衣服和日常食物.
如果你们中有人对他们说,“安心去,保持温暖和丰盛的饮食”,但是对他们的身体需要却一无所获,那有什么好处? 同样地,信仰本身,如果不伴有行动,就已经死亡. (詹姆斯2:15–17,NIV) 死亡的信仰并不能拯救信仰. 也许更大的危险是忽略了我们的内地城市,而不是走在他们的行道上。 大委员会包括我们的内地城市.
然而我们常常忽略这项工作, 相信没有任何模式允许我们在这些社区建立教堂。 但确实有 这是传教士模式。 我们拥有我们所需要的一切:一个来自基督的委托,他在场的承诺,圣灵,上帝之道,一个明确的需要,一个经过考验的模型. 我们该把这个模型放在我们的城市里。

featured.title: Report Cards on Your Actions Won’t Fix Your Heart
featured.summary: From GLP-1s to political reposts to mindfulness streaks, we’re all keeping score. Jesus says you can’t know who you are until you look at your heart.
featured.summary_zh: 我是谁? 所有文化,人类哲学,宗教体系都试图以导致有意义的生活的方式来回答这个问题. 我们想在他们中间找到一条道路,使我们能够说:“我是谁? 我是个好人。
featured.title_zh: 关于您行动的报告卡片无法修复您的心脏
featured.content: Who am I? All cultures, human philosophies, and religious systems try to answer this question in a way that leads to a meaningful life. We want to find in them a path that allows us to say, “Who am I? I’m a good person. I’m someone who is living a good and right life.” What paths toward goodness and righteousness are being offered today? They’re as vast and varied as ever. One popular path is to optimize your life via medical improvements, ranging from plastic surgery to GLP-1s. The more you can “ humanmaxx ” your body to look healthier and be stronger, the more likely you’ll be considered an ideal human being—a good person to hire, to be friends with, to date or marry. Political engagement is another common path. Your goodness is determined by how connected you are to particular political movements. You can feel like you’re a good person when you make sure you quickly like and repost all Zohran Mamdani’s videos. Or alternatively, you’ll be affirmed as a good person by how aggressively you go after or insult people who like Mamdani. Paths our culture offers to the good life are often combined. Your sense of how good a person you are is measured by a mixture of how long you’ve engaged in therapy, how many hours you volunteer at your children’s school, and how long your streak is on your mindfulness app. Tara Isabella Burton, in her book Strange Rites: New Religions for a Godless World , argues that people have formed their own religious systems by drawing from various religions and philosophies. People have become “creators of their own bespoke religions, mixing and matching spiritual and aesthetic and experiential and philosophical traditions.” We’re doing a DIY project, grabbing and piecing together whatever’s around us, hoping we can come up with something to help us in our journey. So, what path does Christianity offer to assure us we’re living a good and righteous life? Keeping Score The Christian approach is to address what the Bible calls the heart. The heart is the Bible’s shorthand term for describing the part of you that drives and motivates you, what dictates your thoughts and emotions. Christianity starts with the heart because this is the only real way by which you can determine who you are and what needs to change. We see the contrast between the religious and cultural approach and the Christian approach in Jesus’s interaction with the Pharisees in Matthew 15:1–20. The Pharisees confront Jesus to ask him why his disciples don’t wash their hands before eating. Handwashing before meals was one of the many religious rules the Pharisees had developed, practiced, and called others to practice. For the Pharisees, the best answer to the question “Who am I?” was based on how well they followed their set standards. If a person kept the standard and had a life that could be observed to follow all the rules, then that person could definitively say to themselves and those around them, “I’m a good person who is living a good and right life.” Jesus’s story about the Pharisee in Luke 18:9–14 is another example. The Pharisee intently notes in his prayer how he, unlike the tax collector praying next to him, fasts twice a week and always gives the full tithe. Jesus describes the Pharisees in Matthew 6 as people who make sure their regular prayers can be seen and affirmed by all. The Pharisees weren’t alone in this approach. Greco-Roman religion had its own rules and standards to follow. Its gods demanded rituals, sacrifices, and festivals to appease and honor them. Performed rightly, they’d result in people securing the blessing they needed from the gods, thus assuring them their lives were good and righteous. Jesus, however, reframes the Pharisees’ questioning by showing that their approach doesn’t go far enough. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. And that means looking at the heart. Jesus says, “What comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart” (Matt. 15:18)—who we are is revealed only when we ask questions that get at the primary motives and desires within our hearts. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. It’s not enough to obey the sixth commandment, “Do not murder,” by simply performing your nonviolent lifestyle to others for their approval. Jesus says we can’t say what kind of person we are until we’ve asked if anger, aggression, or violence reside within our heart (Matt. 5:21–22). Similarly, the Pharisees said that we are to love our neighbor but hate our enemy (Matt. 5:43). But Jesus presses deeper when he tells the parable of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), positing that we aren’t people who love our neighbor unless we’re willing to cross cultural and racial boundaries, to be radically generous, to put ourselves and our resources at risk for the sake of others. And we won’t do those things unless we look beneath our performance and interrogate our hearts. Report-Card Life This heart-based approach remains relevant and helpful to us living within today’s culture. The Pharisaic system and Greco-Roman religion are no longer popularly practiced. But the thought that we can positively answer the question “Who am I?” through external practices and obedience to observable practices remains the norm. Though the standards and the gods look different, people are still looking to “follow the rules” toward becoming a person who lives a good life. It’s just that now there are more options and more bespoke standards. This isn’t to say our modern efforts are insignificant. Many of the examples I listed earlier can bring mental, social, and physical improvements—in some cases better than anything our world has offered before. But the problem remains the same as in Jesus’s day: These efforts ultimately don’t go deep enough. The Christian approach is that being able to know you’re a good person won’t happen by doing more and better things. To answer the question “Who am I?” in a way where I truly know that I’m living a good and right life always begins by asking, “What’s the state of my heart?” Modern trends and philosophies tend to frame life around practices, rituals, procedures, or routines. It’s a report-card framework: How many times have I prayed or meditated this week? How much money have I donated this year? How many times have I worked out this week? From Report Card to Relationship Christianity presents a different framework, one that gets at the heart. Christianity helps us see our hearts through a relational lens: “Whom or what do you worship? Whom or what do you love?” It then leads us to the answer we need for those questions: “We need a heart that will worship and love what’s good and right.” This is why the gospel stands out as the most complete story and the most effective way to answer the question “Who am I?” The doctrine of sin examines our heart and diagnoses the real problem. It shows us how God is the source of all that’s good and right and how human beings, in having sinned against God, are now far away from him. This means that even our best efforts toward being good come up short. The gospel stands out as the most complete story and the most effective way to answer the question, ‘Who am I?’ The doctrine of Christ’s sacrificial death and atonement for sins then shows the way to fix the problem. Christ, in giving up his life and atoning for our sin, bridged the gap between us and God, a bridge we can cross by faith and trust in Christ. Finally, the doctrine of redemption and regeneration by the Holy Spirit shows us that our reconnection to God through Jesus also is about transformation. We get new hearts, ones no longer compromised or enslaved by our sinful motives and desires. These new hearts help us live into what’s good and right, because we now have hearts that truly do worship and love God. As Titus 3:5–6 says, we’re saved “not because of works done by us in righteous

我是谁? 所有文化,人类哲学,宗教体系都试图以导致有意义的生活的方式来回答这个问题. 我们想在他们中间找到一条道路,使我们能够说:“我是谁? 我是个好人。 我是一个过着良好和正确生活的人。 今天为善良和正义提供了哪些途径? 他们和以往一样,
一个通俗的途径是通过医疗改进来优化你的生活,从整形手术到GLP-1. 你越能"人类马克思"你的身体看起来越健康,越强壮,你就越有可能被认为是理想的人——一个能雇佣、成为朋友、约会或结婚的好人。 政治参与是另一条共同道路。
你的善良取决于你和特定政治运动的关系 也觉得自己是个好人, 或以你对马姆达尼的追求或侮辱来证明你是一个好人。 我们的文化为美好生活提供的道路常常是结合在一起的。
你对一个人有多好的感觉,是通过你从事治疗的时间、你在学校志愿工作多少小时、以及你的心智应用上多久来衡量的。
Tara Isabella Burton在她所著"陌生的Rites:新宗教为无神的世界"一书中认为,人们通过从各种宗教和哲学中汲取来形成自己的宗教体系.
人们已经成为“他们自己所讲的宗教的创造者,混合和配合精神和美学以及体验和哲学传统。” 我们正在进行一个DIY计划, 抓取和整理我们周围的东西, 希望我们能想出一些东西来帮助我们的旅程。 基督教给我们提供了什么途径来保证我们过着美好和正义的生活?
记分 基督教的方法是解决"圣经"所说的"心". 心灵是圣经的简称,用来描述你推动和激励你,决定你思想和情绪的部分。 基督教以心为起点,因为这是你决定自己是谁和需要改变的惟一真正方法.
在耶稣与法利赛人的互动中, 法利赛人面对耶稣, 餐前洗手是法利赛人制定,练习的众多宗教规则之一,并号召其他人去练习.
对法利赛人来说,“我是谁?” 问题的最佳答案在于他们遵守既定标准的情况。
如果一个人能遵守标准,并过着可以遵守所有规则的生活,那么这个人可以肯定地对自己和周围的人说,“我是个好人,正在过上良好和正确的生活。” 耶稣在卢克18:9–14中讲述了法利赛人的故事是另一个例子.
法利赛人在祷告中故意记下他如何与旁边的收税者不同的是,他每周斋戒两次并总是给满分之一. 耶稣在"马太福音"6中将法利赛人描述为确保他们的定期祷告能被所有人都看到和肯定的人. 法利赛人并不孤单。 格雷科-罗马宗教有自己的规则和标准可以遵循。
它的神要求举行仪式,祭祀,并举行节日来安抚和尊崇他们. 让他们得到神赐予的祝福, 但耶稣重新定义了法利赛人的质疑,
正确的生活和人类的繁荣需要不止一种外向行动。 这需要更严格的内部检查。 并谓观心相. 耶稣说, " 口出之事从心而来 " (Matt. 15:18)——只有当我们提出我们心中主要动机和愿望的问题时,我们才会被揭穿。
正确的生活和人类的繁荣需要不止一种外向行动。 这需要更严格的内部检查。 仅仅向他人表达非暴力的生活方式, 在问到愤怒、攻击或暴力是否存在于我们的心中之前,
5: 21–22 (英语). 同样,法利赛人说,我们爱我们的邻居,但恨我们的敌人(马特:43)。
但是,耶稣在说好撒玛利亚人的比喻(Luke 10:25-37)时更进一步,假定我们不是热爱邻居的人,除非我们愿意跨越文化和种族界限,彻底慷慨地将我们自己和我们的资源置于危险之中,为他人着想。 我们不会做那些事情, 除非我们看在我们的表演的底部,
报告卡生命 这种以心为本的做法对我们生活在今天的文化中仍然有意义和有帮助。 法利赛克教和格里克-罗马教不再被普遍信奉. 但是,关于我们能够通过外部做法和服从可观察到的做法而积极回答“我是谁?” 的问题的想法仍然是常态。
尽管标准与神看起来不同,人们仍然期待“遵守规则”,成为过上美好生活的人。 现在有更多选择, 这并不是说我们的现代努力微不足道。
我前面列举的许多例子可以带来精神、社会和身体方面的改善——在某些情况下,这些改善比我们世界以前提供的任何改善都好。 但问题与耶稣时代一样: 这些努力最终不够深入。 基督教的观点是, 能够知道你是一个好人,
在回答“我是谁? ”问题时,我真正知道,我正在过着美好和正确的生活,但首先要问,“我的心状况如何?” 现代的趋势和哲学往往会把生活设定在惯例,仪式,程序,或例行公事上. 这是一个报告卡框架: 这周我祈祷或冥想了多少次? 今年我捐了多少钱?
这周我练了多少次? 从"报告卡"到"关系基督教"提供了一个不同的框架,一个得到心脏的框架. 基督教帮助我们通过一种关系视角来看待我们的心:“你们崇拜谁或什么?
你爱谁或什么?” 然后,它引导我们找到我们需要的这些问题的答案 : “ 我们需要一颗会崇拜和热爱美好和正义的心。 ” 这就是为什么福音是回答“我是谁? 罪的学说审视了我们的心脏,诊断出了真正的问题.
它向我们展示了上帝是如何成为一切善和正之源的,以及人类在触犯了上帝之后如何远离他。 这意味着,即使我们为成为好人而作的最好努力也无济于事。
福音是最完整的故事,也是回答这个问题的最有效方法,“我是谁?” 基督的牺牲和对罪的赎罪的学说,然后表明了解决问题的方法。 基督,通过放弃他的生命,为我们的罪孽赎罪,弥合了我们和上帝之间的鸿沟,通过信仰和对基督的信任,我们可以跨越一座桥梁.
最后,圣灵的救赎和再生学说向我们表明,我们通过耶稣与上帝的再接连也是关于转变的. 我们得到了新的心, 不再被我们的罪恶动机和欲望所损害或奴役。 这些新心能帮助我们活到善与正的地步,
正如Titus 3:5-6所言,我们之所以被拯救,并非因为我们在正义中所做的工作。

featured.title_zh: 谁是圣经中的神？
featured.content: According to the Belgic Confession , God reveals himself to us in two “books”: the book of nature (God’s world) and the book of Scripture (God’s written Word). The primary way God reveals himself in the book of Scripture is by proclaiming his name. In this first of two paired lectures from TGC25, Scott Swain considers several of the names whereby God reveals himself in the Bible. Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope. It also helps us better appreciate the ways God reveals himself to us in Jesus Christ. featured.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Finds New Inspiration in an Old Story
featured.summary: ‘I Play Rocky’ is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told.
featured.summary_zh: Rocky在50年前的电影院首映, 1976年, 即刻出演了"一团糟"和"批判亲爱的"(1976年最受欢迎的电影和"最佳相片奥斯卡"得主),从此成为了美国电影院的泛神电影. Rocky的费城设置和衰落, 从富人到富人的故事中抓住了美国令人费解的乐观, 现在在2026年——美国半个世纪. 洛基要重新上演戏剧 而一部新电影,I Play Rocky(今天在部分剧场出演)讲述了偶像电影发展的故事,这部电影是其自身的一出逊色史诗.
featured.title_zh: 《我扮演洛基》在古老的故事中寻找新的灵感
featured.content: Rocky debuted in theaters 50 years ago, in 1976—a bicentennial-year release that underscored the movie’s profound American spirit. Immediately a blockbuster and critical darling (the highest-grossing movie of 1976 and winner of the Best Picture Oscar), it has since become a pantheon film in American cinema. Rocky ’s Philadelphia setting and underdog, rags-to-riches story captured a hardscrabble American optimism, something that gave needed inspiration in the mid-1970s and resonates still today. Now in 2026—America’s semiquincentennial— Rocky is getting a theatrical rerelease. And a new movie, I Play Rocky (out today in select theaters) is telling the story of the iconic movie’s development, which is an underdog epic of its own. The movie, directed by Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) and starring Anthony Ippolito in a breakout turn as Sylvester Stallone, is a refreshingly feel-good crowd pleaser. It’s the sort of well-made, intelligent, but also inspiring movie for grown-ups that feels like a dying breed in Hollywood. Movies About Moviemaking I Play Rocky (rated PG-13 for language) follows a well-worn template of a movie about the making of a classic movie. Saving Mr. Banks (2013) was about Walt Disney and the making of Mary Poppins . Hitchcock (2012) was about Alfred Hitchcock and the making of Psycho . Last year’s Nouvelle Vague was about Jean-Luc Godard and the making of Breathless . I Play Rocky is about Stallone and the making of Rocky . Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Self-reflexive inspiration goes back more than a century in cinema, perhaps starting with Dziga Vertov’s Man with a Movie Camera (1929). The 1950s produced classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Singin’ in the Rain (1952), but the trend really picked up in the postmodern era in the 1960s and beyond: 8 ½ (1963), Day for Night (1973), Mulholland Drive (2001), Adaptation (2002), The Artist (2011), and Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood (2019). The list is long. A hallmark of postmodernity is a metaposture of knowing awareness—storytellers who know they’re storytellers and want the audience to know that they know. As postmodernism has given way to metamodernism , the trend of “movies about moviemaking” has continued, but in a slightly different register. These sorts of films are no longer merely metaexercises in self-awareness. The cerebral, cynical detachment of “films about filmmaking” like Barton Fink (1991), Ed Wood (1994), or even Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) has given way to metamodern expressions that blend cynicism and sincerity, self-awareness with earnest escapism. Steven Spielberg’s The Fabelmans (2022) is a recent example of a movie in this vein, and I Play Rocky has a similar feel. Even as it lifts the veil on the Hollywood myth factory and mines many laughs out of the fundamentally profit-seeking, money-centric nature of the movie business, it’s full of heart and soul. It has a joyful, hopeful, sincere, perhaps idealistic spirit (“I’d rather be an optimist and be wrong, than a pessimist and be right,” one character says). Refreshing Celebration of Marriage I also like how I Play Rocky celebrates the empowering beauty of marriage. The film opens with Stallone as a broke actor in New York, sometimes sleeping on the streets and at one point accepting a role in an X-rated adult film just to earn some desperately needed money (a dark part of Stallone’s past that the film plays for awkward laughs). He’s a lost soul with bleak prospects. But then he meets Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), with whom he works at a movie theater. They get married and move to Los Angeles, and things start to turn around for him. As a husband and soon a father, Stallone feels more urgency to provide. He valets at a swanky Hollywood restaurant to pay the bills while he churns out scripts that he tries to get into influential hands. Sasha types the scripts for him and encourages him at every turn, even as they struggle to pay rent. At one point, she reminds him, “It’s not just you against the world. It’s us against the world.” She’s his ally and cheerleader, believing in him when few else do. Stallone’s parents were divorced, and he had a complicated relationship with his father, Frank (Matt Dillon). Yet I Play Rocky doesn’t play the “blame my parents for all my trauma” card—which is also refreshing. At one point, Stallone says, “My dad, he messed up a lot. But it’s my life.” Stallone doesn’t blame anyone else for the bad choices he’s made or the setbacks he’s had. His story is his own. At a time when it seems every other movie is some version of therapeutic moral absolution for sinners and villains , on account of their broken upbringing, it’s nice to have a movie that pushes back against this. “It’s my story,” Stallone tells the producers who want to turn his Rocky script into a film. “So I play Rocky.” Searching for Stories We used to just tell stories. Now we tell stories about stories. We write books about story and the spiritual deprivation of a destoried world . We hunger for old stories but struggle to invent new ones . Hence the appeal of a movie like I Play Rocky , which finds new narrative inspiration only by mining a classic. Our contemporary world is so uprooted, so unplaced in space and time, so rattled and wearied by what Hartmut Rosa calls “ social acceleration ,” that we feel removed or alienated from our own stories. We’re simultaneously hyperskeptical of the stories we’re told (you see this clearly in the popularity of You Can See Everything ) and deeply hungry to find our own story, to be situated in a compelling narrative that’s going somewhere and has redemption, purpose, a point. This is metamodernism’s complicated relationship with story. There’s still a residual postmodern skepticism about all stories and storytelling, but also a growing recognition that we can’t live outside of stories and storytelling—at least in the subjective, “my story” sense. There’s still a residual postmodern skepticism about all stories and storytelling, but also a growing recognition that we can’t live outside of stories and storytelling. Perhaps it’s downstream from social media turning us all into performers for audiences, but it feels like there’s a pressure to “find your story” (a.k.a. your brand/niche), own it, and guard it from others who might want to manipulate or leverage it for their purposes. The 2026 comedy Power Ballad touches on some of these themes of creative ownership, as does Taylor Swift in her “Taylor’s Version” series of rerecorded albums. The recent movie Digger explores the way creative control and story-crafting can be PR—shaping one’s image or the reputation of someone you love. I Play Rocky is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told. As much as this sort of storytelling is pitched as empowerment and agency, however, it also feels burdensome and exhausting. Do we really find freedom when we’re constantly obsessing over our story, or our backstory (e.g. TikTok “lore drop” trend ), and how it’s perceived by online fans and followers? The story poverty in today’s world won’t find a satisfying resolution in hyperindividuated narrative obsession. What we really need is a grander story—something bigger than “my story,” bigger than your story. What’s truly freeing is not owning our own story but seeing ourselves as part of God’s story—owned by him, our lives not our own. This is our only hope in life and death .

真正自由的不是我们自己的故事, 而是将自己视为上帝故事的一部分, 这是我们对生死的唯一希望

featured.title: How the Lord’s Supper Fuels Spiritual Growth
featured.summary: Calvin shows us that the Lord’s Supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time.

featured.title_zh: 主的晚餐如何促进灵性成长
featured.content: Recently, I (and my peers) have experienced a number of parishioners converting to Catholicism. As I’ve talked to these converts, they’ve consistently brought up the Lord’s Table. They find encouragement in identifying the bread and wine with Jesus’s body and blood. I’ve heard statements such as this: Pastor George, I like the idea that Jesus was talking about the Lord’s supper when he said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). My faith just feels more real if I’m literally bringing Jesus into my body on a daily basis. While this phenomenon seems to be happening with greater frequency, it’s not totally new. Years ago, I served alongside a man at an ordination service for another pastor in our city. I hadn’t met this man before; I only knew he had until recently been a professor at a Reformed and evangelical seminary. This man preached a solid message on Jesus’s call for ministers of the gospel, and I thanked him for it. Then, the next day, I saw him being interviewed on TV. I tuned in just as he explained, I needed more realism than my tradition provided, so during lunch I would walk down to the local Roman Catholic parish and take the Eucharist. To unite literally with Jesus’s body and blood was more deeply satisfying to me than the “mystery of union with Christ” my church taught. So, I resigned my post at the seminary and went home to Rome. I could relate other conversations with those who have left the Reformed faith and joined the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglo-Catholic traditions. A similar theme runs through them all: the desire for a more transformational, sensory reality than what the Reformed view of the Lord’s supper provides. Is this critique valid? How would John Calvin respond to the critique that if you follow the Reformed view of the supper, you’re missing out on its power? Transformed at the Table Sometimes, in an effort to have biblically faithful theology, Reformed Christians speak only of what the communion elements are not . I’m painfully aware of my of shortcomings in this regard. This can inadvertently drive some believers to seek out a more “real” experience in other traditions. We can get caught up in debating the exact nature of the bread and wine and forget to ask the more pressing question: How should this meal change me today? Let’s look back at Calvin’s teachings on communion. When we do, we’ll recover a renewed vision for the table, one that sees it as a divine encounter that motivates a transformed life of profound gratitude and obedience. In short, Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In Calvin’s “ Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper ,” he writes that the supper fuels the believer’s spiritual growth in at least three ways. 1. The supper assures us of our inheritance in Christ. Calvin teaches that Jesus uses his table to assure us of our inheritance. He doesn’t merely mean that the supper gives us a psychological boost. He means that assurance comes by means of a real union between Christ and the believer, and he means that our experience of this union is expedited by faithfully partaking in the covenant meal. Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In his commentary on Ephesians, Calvin writes , “Paul says that we are members of his [Christ’s] flesh and of his bones. Do we wonder then, that in the Lord’s Supper he holds out his body to be enjoyed by us, and to nourish us unto eternal life?” Calvin insists that by faith, Christians are made members of Jesus’s fleshly human body, so at communion, we experience all the benefits of spiritual union with him. Christ took on flesh so that in his ascended state, he might be a channel of righteousness to the believer, pouring into him all that Christ’s human life accomplished. As a result of Jesus’s incarnation and death, God the Father established what Calvin calls a “holy brotherhood” between his Son and those united to his human flesh in salvation. What assurance! 2. The supper confirms and increases faith. Calvin sees the supper as a public and dramatic statement that God has atoned for the sins of the elect. God gives us this dramatic reenactment because he loves us. He knows “our faith is slight and feeble” and “unless it be propped up on all sides and sustained by every means, it trembles, wavers, totters, and at last gives way.” The Lord’s supper is a God-ordained means of “propping up” our faith, not because the supper is necessary to confirm God’s Word but because it improves our faith. In the supper, we experience a dramatic reenactment in which the ascended Christ, through his Holy Spirit, lifts our hearts to heaven. Christ does this for us, Calvin says, because regular communion with him strengthens us for the spiritual discouragements that inevitably come through besetting sin, temptation, and trials. Calvin views the sacraments as a means that cause Christ to “grow in us” so that our faith is fed more and more with Christ himself. Christians may experience any number of trials throughout their weeks that cause Christ’s spiritual, unseen realities to feel less plausible and real. Yes, our weak faith “trembles, wavers, and totters.” But when we come to the table, Christ gives us a public, dramatic reenactment that confirms his reality to our consciences and increases our faith. 3. The supper motivates and enables obedient Christian living. Calvin says, “There cannot be a spur which can pierce us more to the quick than when He makes us, so to speak, see with the eye, touch with the hand, and distinctly perceive the inestimable blessing of feeding on His own substance.” Thus, at the table, says Calvin, we’re compelled to a new obedience rooted in a grateful response to the blessings we receive there in Christ. Calvin’s conviction that the Lord’s supper provides occasion for this grateful celebration and response led him to structure worship services with this emphasis. In Calvin’s order of worship, the whole service is one long expression of gratitude in which the worshiper brings every aspect of his sin-sickness to the Savior. It concludes at the table where believers gratefully witness the Lord’s healing of all diseases dramatized. Calvin wouldn’t allow worshipers to enjoy this gratitude in private, because it’s a gift to share and a motivation that fuels outward and practical acts of “faith and charity” to others. This aspect of the supper that drives the worshiper closer to his brothers and sisters in Christ is the final distinctive of Calvin’s sacramental theology. Living Out Our Union with Christ As Christ, from love, pours out his life for the believer, the believer also pours out his life for others. So, each time you take the Lord’s supper by faith, you live out of your union with Christ, and he lives in and through you, making you new. Each time you take the Lord’s supper by faith, you live out of your union with Christ, and he lives in and through you, making you new. So, the next time you come to the Lord’s table, come expectantly. The living, risen Christ will use communion as fuel for your spiritual growth.
featured.content_zh:
最近,我(和我的同龄人)经历了一些皈依天主教的教区人士. 当我和这些皈依者交谈时, 他们发现鼓励用耶稣的身体和血液来识别面包和葡萄酒。
我听到过这样的话:乔治牧师,我喜欢耶稣在谈论主的晚餐,他说:“谁吃我的肉喝我的血,谁在我体内,我就在他体内”(John 6:56)。 如果我每天把耶稣带入我的身体, 虽然这种现象似乎更频繁地发生,
多年前,我和一个男人一起 为我们市的另一位牧师服务 我之前从未见过这个人;我只知道他直到最近才成为一所改革后福音神学院的教授。 这个人在耶稣号召福音的大臣们时宣扬一个坚实的信息,我为此感谢他. 然后,第二天,我看到他接受电视采访。
正如他所解释的,我需要比传统更现实的, 所以在午餐期间,我会走进罗马天主教当地的教区, 并带上尤查里会。 比起教会教义的“与基督结合的谜团”, 于是我辞去神学院的职务,回到了罗马.
我可以和那些脱离改革后信仰并加入罗马天主教、东正教或天主教传统的人交谈。 一个类似的主题贯穿于所有这些方面:渴望一个比改革后对主的晚餐提供的看法更具有转型性、感官性的现实。 这种批评有道理吗?
约翰·卡尔文会如何回应这种批评:如果你遵循改革后的晚餐观, 有时候,为了实现圣经上忠实的神学,改革后的基督徒只谈论圣餐的内容。 我痛苦地意识到我在这方面的缺点。
这可能无意中驱使一些信徒在其他传统中寻求更“真实”的经验。 我们可以在辩论面包和葡萄酒的确切性质时陷入困境,并忘记提出更紧迫的问题: 今天这顿饭怎么能改变我? 让我们回顾加尔文关于圣餐的教义。
我们将会重新恢复对桌子的憧憬, 简言之,加尔文告诉我们,主的晚餐是精神成长的燃料,因此,我们每次都应该期待地来到餐桌旁。
他写道, 晚餐至少以三种方式促进信徒的精神成长。 1. 晚餐保证了我们在基督的遗产。 加尔文教耶稣用桌子保证我们的遗产 他不只是说晚餐会给我们心理上的刺激。
他的意思是,通过基督和信徒之间的真正结合来保证,他的意思是,通过忠实地分享契约之餐来加快我们这一结合的经验。 加尔文向我们展示,主的晚餐是精神成长的燃料,因此,我们应当期待在每一次的餐桌上就餐。
Calvin在其对以弗所发表的评论中写道:“保罗说,我们是他[基督]肉体和骨头的成员。
难道我们不知道,在主的晚餐中,他伸出他的身体,让我们享受,并使我们获得永生吗? 加尔文坚持认为,根据信仰,基督徒是耶稣肉体上的身体的成员,因此在圣餐时,我们体验到与他精神结合的所有好处.
基督将肉体取而代之,这样,在他升起的状态下,他可能成为信仰者的正义之道,将基督人类生命所成就的一切注入他体内. 由于耶稣的化身和死亡,"上帝之父"建立了加尔文所称的"神圣的兄弟情谊",他的儿子和那些在救赎中与他的人类肉团结在一起的人之间. 什么保证! 2. 联合国
晚餐证实了并增加了信心. 加尔文认为晚宴是公开和戏剧性的声明,上帝为选举人的罪孽赎罪了. 上帝给了我们这个戏剧性的重现 因为他爱我们。
他知道“我们的信仰轻而易举”和“除非它四面穿梭,用各种手段维持,否则它会颤抖、动摇、起伏,最后让位”。 主的晚餐是上帝授意的“巩固”我们信仰的手段,不是因为晚餐是确认上帝之道所必需,而是因为它提高了我们的信仰。
在晚餐中,我们体验了戏剧性的再现,其中被升起的基督通过他的圣灵将我们的心提升到天堂. 加尔文说,基督这样做是为了我们, 因为与他定期的圣餐会会加强我们的精神阻力, 这些精神阻力不可避免地通过纠缠罪孽,诱惑和考验。
加尔文将圣事视为使基督“成长于我们”的手段,使我们的信仰越来越多地被基督本身所接受。 基督教徒在他们的几周里可能经历许多考验,
是的,我们软弱的信仰“三联、一波又一波地”。 但是,当我们来到议席上时,基督给了我们一个公开的,戏剧性的再现,证实了他对我们良知的现实,并增加了我们的信仰. 3. 晚餐激励并促成服从基督教的生活。
加尔文说 , “ 没有比他造就我们更能快速地击穿我们的一击的了, 可以说,用眼睛看,用手触摸, 并清楚地看到用他自己的物质来喂食的不可估量的祝福。 ” 因此,加尔文说,在座各位,我们被迫重新服从,这植根于对基督所赐福的感激之情。
加尔文相信主的晚餐为这一感恩的庆典和回应提供了契机,因此他以此为重心构建了礼拜服务. 在加尔文的崇拜秩序中,整个礼拜是长期表达的感激之情,在这种感谢中,崇拜者将他的罪恶症的方方面面带给救世主.
最后,信徒们感谢地见证了上帝治愈了戏剧化的所有疾病。 加尔文不允许崇拜者私下享受这种感恩,因为它是一种分享的礼物,是一种动机,可以助长对外和实际上的“信仰和慈善”行为。
晚餐的这个方面促使崇拜者在基督中更接近他的兄弟姐妹,是加尔文神圣神学的最后特色. 与基督同生共生,从爱为信徒倾出生命,信徒也为他人倾出生命.
所以,每次你用信仰来吃主的晚餐,你都与基督一起生活,他住在你体内并透过你,让你成为新人。 每次你以信仰接受主的晚餐时,你都与基督一起生活,他住在你体内并穿过你,使你成为新人。 所以,下一次你来到上帝的桌子, 期待。
活着的,升起的基督会用圣餐作为你精神成长的燃料.

featured.title: Editor’s Pick: New Children’s Picture Books
featured.summary: Let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment and, even as it changes to something new, that God’s goodness is everlasting.
featured.summary_zh: 秋为一季之变. 在家中,随着叶子被黄了,日子被缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学. 这意味着图书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激 来的新事物。 这些书中很多是关于大变化并适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心.
featured.title_zh: 编辑精选：全新儿童图画书
featured.content: Autumn is a season of changes. At our home, as the leaves yellowed and the days shortened, my youngest child started middle school. That means picture books have me feeling a little nostalgia for the past these days, right alongside a lot of excitement for new things to come. Many of these books are about big changes and adjusting to them, like living with a new baby, moving to a new place, or finding a new heart in Christ’s kingdom. But some are also about the little changes happening around us every day, like laughter over a fleeting moment of childhood imagination or settling down to sleep to prepare for a new day. With all these experiences arriving on the horizon and then flying past like interstate billboards, it’s sweet to remember that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). As you hand one of these brand-new books to a young reader or curl up to enjoy it together, let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment, even as it is changing to something new, and that God’s goodness is everlasting. 1. God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard, illustrated by Bethan Welby ( TGC Store | Amazon) When our family was exhausted and planning a big move with four children ages 6 and under, I really could have used this little book from Betsy Childs Howard. God Gives Sleep is a rhyming board book with illustrations of adorable animals (sleeping ladybugs!) and two simple refrains that even very young listeners can repeat or “read” for themselves: “God gives sleep” and “God will keep.” Both reflect promises from God that feel vital to the early days of parenting filled with sweet, sleepy snuggles and long, sleepless nights. The last picture shows the entire family asleep and includes Isaiah 40:31 (“Those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength,” NIV). God Gives Sleep is engaging, gentle, funny, and wise, and I’ve already given it to parents of new babies. 2. Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel by A. A. Milne, adapted by Kevan Chandler and Joe Sutphin ( Amazon ) Full disclosure: I’m a huge Pooh fan. I’ve probably read the original Milne book dozens of times, and I can be a little sniffy about adaptations. But I loved this one. While I missed Milne’s distinctive narration in parts of the storytelling, this graphic novel retains enough of the original language and has such beautiful artwork that it easily justifies its existence. Parents of young independent readers often ask me for recommendations for books complex enough to be engaging but with content and formatting suitable for early elementary school. This version perfectly fits that space where 6-to-9-year-olds can track the story through the pictures but also enjoy the challenge of some complex vocabulary (“Sudden and Temporary Immersion”) and jokes that reward context research (“An ambush is a sort of Surprise.” “So is a gorse-bush sometimes.”). Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel is a sweet and worthy tribute to this classic celebration of early childhood in all its imaginative wonder. 3. The Upside-Down, Inside-Out, Can’t-Believe-It Kingdom by Jonathan Landry Cruse, illustrated by Joe Hox ( Amazon ) The adventure begins with a son begging his father to tell him an exciting bedtime story with dragons and knights. The result is this retelling of the gospel as a quest with a king and a prince and a reminder of our humble place in the kingdom. Joe Hox’s illustrations stand out for being traditional and bright, with a dragon that isn’t too fierce for younger readers but also enough detail within the pictures to engage older readers. The story tells us that the good King will “make us be strong with the strength of His might,” a powerful message for young knights who want to do great things for the kingdom. 4. Doing Something New: A Prayer for Beginnings by Mitali Perkins, illustrated by Andrés Landazábal ( Amazon ) Mitali Perkins includes a note in the back of Doing Something New about how she moved many times in childhood: “By the time we settled in California for seventh grade, we had lived in India, Ghana, Cameroon, England, Mexico, and New York.” Changes often come with both losses and gains, and Perkins writes with sympathy and encouragement for children walking through all sorts of new experiences. The text reminds readers to live like Jesus—showing love, courage, and kindness—with the knowledge that Jesus also walked through hard experiences and that he’s with us now, wherever we go. The pictures include what appear to be a new school, new friends, new seasons, and the potential loss of or separation from a loved one. The rhyming words offer this prayer to Christ as a resource for others experiencing changes—“You trusted God and God helped you / Here I am, Lord—help me too.” Also check out these books: Jude and the Extraordinary, Spectacular, Miraculous Day: A Creative Retelling of the Feeding of the 5,000 by Jessica Dennis Bush features beautiful mosaic illustrations that look refreshingly like real art rather than AI and a message about offering Jesus what we have. ( TGC Store | Amazon ) Made like Me: A True Story from the Beginning of Everything by Jen Wilkin (with illustrations by Rommel Ruiz) tells the story of the creation of the world with vibrant, kinetic illustrations and an emphasis on how we were designed for community from the beginning of time. ( TGC Store | Amazon ) The Mansoul Chronicles, Book 2: The Schemes and Snares of Diabolus by Tyler Van Halteren (with illustrations by Uyen Nguyen and Aleksander Jasinski) is an illustrated chapter book retelling a John Bunyan story from the 1600s with surprisingly relevant themes for Christians today. ( Amazon ) The Sweetest of Lemons by Daniel Nayeri (with illustrations by Rahele Jomepour Bell) is both a true story and a fairy tale about “a lemon so perfectly sweet it cured sadness itself.” Like the best fairy stories, it carries themes of courage, perseverance, longing, and—most importantly—hope, acknowledging hardship but resting in the certainty of goodness on the horizon. ( Amazon ) Where Wonder Leads: An Adventure in God’s Wild and Wonderful World by Eryn Lynum (with illustrations by Chiara Fedele) is from the host of the Nat Theo podcast and somehow manages to touch on grief, nature activities, profound theology, and fascinating scientific facts in just over 100 illustrated pages. ( Amazon )
featured.content_zh:
秋为一季之变. 在家中,随着叶子被黄了,日子被缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学. 这意味着图书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激 来的新事物。
这些书中很多是关于大变化并适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心. 但有些人也谈到我们周围每天发生的小变化,比如在童年短暂的想象中欢笑,或者沉睡以准备新的一天。
随着所有这些经历的到来,然后像州际告示牌一样飞过,令人欣慰的是,“每一个好的礼物和完美的礼物都是来自上面,来自灯之父,与他一起没有变化或阴影。” (詹姆斯1:17)。
当你把这些全新的书交给一个年轻的读者 或整理起来一起欣赏的时候, 让这些故事提醒你享受这一刻的美好, 即使它正在变成新的事物, 上帝的善良是永恒的。 1. 联合国
由Bethan Welby(TGC Store QQ Amazon)所展示, 当家庭精疲力竭,计划一个大动作 四个孩子6岁和6岁以下, 我真的可以用这本小书 从贝茜 Childs Howard。
上帝赐予睡眠(God Gives Sleep)是一本配有可爱动物(sleeping ladybugs!)插图的韵律板书,还有两个简单的节奏,即使非常年轻的听众也能为自己重复或“阅读 ” : “ 上帝赐予睡眠 ” 和“上帝会保留 ” 。 两者都反映了上帝的诺言,这些诺言对养育孩子的早期至关重要,充满了甜蜜的,沉睡的和漫长的,无眠的夜晚.

featured.title: How Memorizing the Sermon on the Mount Reorders My Heart
featured.summary: In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount.
featured.summary_zh: 几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上赛门(Matt. 5-7). 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年里, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最出名的布道当作记忆更具有变革性。 约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道:"山上赛蒙是[耶稣]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的东西,因为这是他自己对追随者所希望的和所要做的事的描述".
featured.title_zh: 背诵登山宝训如何重塑我的心
featured.content: A couple of years ago, two college students challenged me—a woman in her 50s—to memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7). Inwardly, I balked, but now I know that few things in my 35 years of following Jesus have been more transformative than committing Jesus’s most famous sermon to memory. John Stott wrote that the Sermon on the Mount is “the nearest thing to a manifesto that [Jesus] ever uttered, for it is his own description of what he wanted his followers to be and to do.” After spending the last few years memorizing it, I see with increasing clarity that I need Jesus’s help to live out what he taught. In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount. Create a New Algorithm The algorithm often knows us better than we know ourselves. Every time we buy something on Amazon or pause to watch a reel on social media, the algorithm chronicles our activities and builds a profile of us. This profile shows our real interests (not just the ones we list in our social media bios) and some of our most private behaviors (the ones we thank God aren’t live streamed). In milliseconds, companies use what the algorithm knows about us to discover the most effective way to get us to buy their products. In the same way that the algorithm learns about us with each post we like and each reel we watch, God’s Word comes alive in us with every command we learn and put into practice, with every verse we ponder, and with every teaching we adopt as a way of life. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Let Scripture Reorder Your Heart Before I started my memorization project, I’d heard many Christians tout Scripture memory as one of the most potent tools for conforming to Jesus, but I didn’t take it seriously. All that changed when I realized algorithms had more access to my life than God’s Word did. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Like many Americans, I was averaging more than two hours daily scrolling social media and shopping online, and much less time reading the Bible. I’d thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. Memorizing and studying the Sermon on the Mount has provided a powerful reset. I’ve noticed two significant changes in my life. 1. My thoughts are increasingly populated by Jesus’s desires for me. Previously, I was easily shaped by what internet influencers said I should be doing and what my heart really wanted to do. Now, Scripture tenderly draws me to Christ’s transforming grace. For example, a few months ago, someone wrote harsh words to me. I couldn’t sidestep what I’d memorized: Pray for those who hurt you (Mt. 5:44) In those difficult interactions, Jesus’s teaching gave me wisdom to stop reacting and start praying for the one lashing out. Pausing to pray breaks down my self-protective stance so I can consider what the log in my eye might be (Mt. 7:5). 2. I see how vastly different God’s kingdom is from the world we live in. I no longer feel as drawn to the shallow version of perfection the algorithm offers me—the beautiful home, the perfectly fit woman charmingly dressed, or the promise of perpetual travel. When I stop to linger over another picture-perfect kitchen, the Sermon on the Mount prompts me to consider where my treasure really is. These chapters have given me a robust lens through which I can view all of God’s Word. After drinking so deeply of Jesus’s sermon , I see it as the hinge on which both the Old Testament and the New Testament hang. I had thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. When Jesus equates murder with anger, he exposes a corruption we prefer not to acknowledge within ourselves (Matt. 5:21–26). Later in the New Testament, we see we have a Savior who forgives our anger and frees us to live to God’s glory. Having this framework embedded in my mind helps me remember the gospel when outside influences pull my attention away. The first three years of my journey into the Sermon on the Mount have helped me be more like Jesus. Yet it’s obvious to me that my journey has just begun. My life changed when those two college students challenged me to memorize the sermon. Almost every day, those words draw me closer to my Savior and encourage me to conform to him. The Sermon on the Mount has given me more joy than any product the algorithm could ever pop into my newsfeed.

几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上赛门(Matt. 5-7). 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年里, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最出名的布道当作记忆更具有变革性。
约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道:"山上赛蒙是[耶稣]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的东西,因为这是他自己对追随者所希望的和所要做的事的描述". 我越来越清楚地看到,我需要耶稣的帮助来维持他所教的。
在一个算法捕捉到我们感情并通过我们的渴望来引诱我们上线的世界中,我们可以采用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习并记住"圣经"——特别是"山上"的"塞尔门". 创建新算法 算法常常比我们自己更了解我们.
每次我们购买亚马逊或暂停观看社交媒体的片段, 算法记录我们的活动, 以及一些最私人的行为(我们感谢上帝的人不是活生生的)。
在毫秒内,公司利用算法了解我们的情况,发现最有效的方法让我们购买他们的产品. 正如算法用我们所喜欢的每一个帖子和我们所看的每一卷片子来了解我们一样,上帝的言语以我们所学习和运用的每一个命令、我们所思考的每一个诗句和我们所采纳的作为生活方式的每一个教义,在我们中充满活力。
通过吸收和服从耶稣在"山上"的赛蒙,我们可以建立一个反馈回路,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 在开始我的回忆计划之前, 我听到许多基督徒将圣经记忆说成是符合耶稣的最有力工具之一,
当我意识到算法与上帝的言语相比, 通过吸收和服从耶稣在"山上"的赛蒙,我们可以建立一个反馈回路,扩大他的王国对我们生活的统治. 我和许多美国人一样,平均每天有两个多小时 滚动社交媒体和网上购物, 阅读圣经的时间要少得多。
我本以为没有时间是我记起圣经的最大障碍。 但实际上,我的爱和优先考虑是障碍。 纪念并研究了"山上"的"塞尔门"提供了强大的重置. 我注意到我生命中有两个重大的变化。 1. 耶稣对我的渴望使我的思想日益丰富。
之前,我很容易被网络影响者 说我应该做什么 和我的心真正想要做什么。 现在,《圣经》轻而易举地吸引我走向基督的恩典。 例如,几个月前,有人给我写了严厉的话. 我无法回避我所记住的:为伤害你的人祈祷(Mt.
5:44 在困难的交往中,耶稣的教导给了我智慧,让我停止反应,开始为那一次狂欢祈祷. 暂停祈祷 打破自我保护的姿势 这样我就可以考虑我的眼中可能是什么(7:5山) 2. 我看到上帝的王国与我们生活的世界大相径庭。
我不再觉得算法能吸引到我的 浅薄的完美版本, 当我停止停留 停留在另一个图片完美的厨房, 山上赛门 促使我考虑 我的宝藏到底在哪里。
这些章节给了我一个强烈的透镜,我可以透视上帝的所有言语。 在饮用耶稣的布道之后,我认为这是旧约和新约所依赖的。 我以为没有时间 是我记起圣经的最大障碍 但实际上,我的爱和优先考虑是障碍。
当耶稣将谋杀与愤怒等同起来时,他揭露了我们不愿承认的腐败(Matt. 5:21-26)。 稍后在"新约"中,我们看到我们有一个救世主,他宽恕了我们的愤怒,使我们自由活在上帝的荣耀下. 将这个框架嵌入我的脑海里, 有助于我记住福音, 当外部影响吸引我的注意力。
我进入山上赛门的最初三年帮助我更像耶稣. 但对我来说, 当两个大学生要求我记住布道时,我的生活就变了。 几乎每一天,这些话都使我更接近我的救世主,鼓励我服从他.
山上赛蒙给我的欢乐 比算法上的任何产品都多

featured.title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
featured.content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. We pray the second petition of the Lord’s Prayer (“Thy kingdom come”) with the fifth petition also in mind (“Forgive us our debts”). Pray with a Desire for Repentance If God could turn his anger away from repentant sinners in exile (Ps. 79:5), then he could do the same for Israel’s enemies. While this is not explicit in Psalm 79, its near neighbor Psalm 83, at the conclusion of this section of Asaph psalms, prays that God would fill the faces of these enemy nations with shame “that they might seek [the LORD’s name]” (v. 16). It is legitimate to see this desire as qualifying the earlier imprecations in the Asaph collection (indeed, in the whole Psalter). Hamilton even suggests every prayer for judgment in the psalms should be read as if containing an implicit “footnote” desiring repentance as a possibility. Pray with the Hope of Final Justice The prayers of judgment, like Psalm 79, are not petty prayers incompatible with a Christian ethic. God’s people pray in response to horrific injustice, aimed at the glory of God, with a posture of humility and openness to their enemies becoming God’s friends. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. The imprecatory psalms, then, fit perfectly with the gospel of Jesus Christ. And they arm the church to intercede for the saints in a day when our Christian brothers and sisters suffer great harm throughout the world. We long for God to answer these prayers through the conversion of our enemies. But if they remain impenitent, it is only right for God to bring justice. And it is thus right for us to pray that he would.

祈求对骇人听闻的不公正行为做出回应, 他们玷污了上帝的圣址,把信主的肉献给大地的野兽,他们把血洒得像水一样,并拒绝给他们安葬,这是真主的宗族变成他们的邻居的恶言。
诗篇79不是针对小不满而祈祷的,而是源于可怕的邪恶。 诗篇79不是针对小的不满而祈祷的,而是源于可怕的邪恶。 这有两个影响。 首先,这些祷告不能让我们允许我们对任何人祈祷这些事情。
第二,如果我们反对这种祷告,他们要求我们问我们是否曾遇到过任何与导致这种祷告的令人痛苦的罪恶相近的事情。
正如Jamie Grant所说 , “ 也许我们不愿接受敌意的诗句, 如果我们知道"诗经79"所说的恐怖(以及我们受迫害的兄弟姐妹每天忍受的恐怖),
祈求上帝的荣耀, 我们从《诗经》79:6中看到这一点。 在那里,各国拒绝呼唤上帝的名声是Asaph哭喊的动机。 同样,第9节引用了上帝的光荣及其 " 名字的缘故 " 作为上帝回应这一要求的理由。
第10节担心的是,目前,目光灿烂的国家说,“他们的上帝在哪里?” 因此,阿萨夫要求将上帝的公义在列国中公之于众(v. 10),并让真主的宗族赞颂他(v.13). 神的荣耀是圣诗的终极结局.
或如詹姆斯·汉密尔顿所说,“通过判断拯救上帝的荣耀是诗歌神学的中心。” 般若菩萨摩诃萨七十九. 他们的欲望是“尊贵的, 以蓬勃姿态祈祷 神圣的诗歌不是本着自以为是的精神祈祷的;祈祷者理解他们对上帝恩惠的需要。
他们以谦卑姿态祈祷正义,他们承认,除了上帝的恩惠之外,这种判决也是他们应得的(vv.8-9)。 这与寡妇在路加福音18:1-8中为正义祈祷, 我们祈祷正义,但我们这样做是宽恕罪人。
我们祈祷主祷告的第二份请愿书(“Thy Kingdom coming”),第五项请愿书也铭记在心(“为我们的债务道歉”)。 如果上帝能把愤怒从流放的悔罪者身上移开(第79:5页),
虽然这在Psalm 79中并不明确,但它的近邻Psalm 83在Asaph psalms这一节结尾祈祷上帝会以耻辱填满这些敌国的脸,"以便他们寻求[耶和华之名]"(v.16). 将这种愿望视为对阿萨夫收藏(事实上,整个Psalter)中早先的杂音加以限定是合理的.
汉密尔顿甚至建议在圣诗中每一次为判断祈祷,都应理解为包含一个隐含的“脚注”,希望能够悔改。 与最终正义的希望一起祈祷 判断的祈祷,如诗篇79,不是与基督教伦理格格不入的微小祈祷.
上帝的人民祈祷,以应对可怕的不公正,以上帝的荣耀为目标,以谦卑和对敌人开放的姿态成为上帝的朋友。 我们祈祷正义,但我们这样做是宽恕罪人。 浸礼诗,那么,完全符合耶稣基督的福音.
他们武装教堂 来替圣徒们说情 在我们的基督徒兄弟姐妹 在世界各地遭受重大伤害的一天里 我们渴望上帝通过改变我们的敌人来回应这些祈祷. 但是如果他们保持无礼,上帝就应该伸张正义。 因此,我们祈祷他会这样做是正确的。

featured.title: Martin Luther in 5 Latin Phrases
featured.summary: Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift.
featured.summary_zh: 马丁·路德于1483年11月10日出生于德国艾斯莱本. 第二天他在圣彼得和保罗教堂被洗礼. 7岁时,路德进入曼斯菲尔德拉丁学校. 他在那里学习了拉丁语的语法和祷告,并记住了伊索普的寓言。
featured.title_zh: 马丁·路德的5个拉丁短语
featured.content: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben, Germany, on November 10, 1483. He was christened at Saints Peter and Paul Church the next day. At age 7, Luther entered the Mansfeld Latin School. There he learned Latin grammar and prayers, and he memorized Aesop’s Fables . From those early years through his time studying at boarding school in Magdeburg then later at the University of Erfurt, Luther was a diligent student. He kept up with his Latin, and several important Latin phrases appear throughout Luther’s writings. Five of them serve as a good summary of his life and chief theological emphases. 1. Iustitia Dei In July 1505, Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm. Panicked and terrified, he bargained with God, promising to become a monk. After entering the monastery, Luther was again overcome by fear. When he led his first mass as a priest, it wasn’t an occasion of joy. Instead, it was filled with trembling. As the service began, Luther took his place at the front of the chapel, and he began to recite the Latin prayers. Luther knew that God is perfect in judgment and completely without sin. So as he thought about iustitia Dei , “the righteousness of God” (Rom. 1:17), terror struck him. Biographer Roland H. Bainton describes the thoughts that plagued Luther’s mind: Who am I that I should . . . raise my hands to the divine Majesty? The angels surround him. At his nod the earth trembles . . . [but] I am dust and ashes. When Luther held up the bread and wine, he shook so badly he almost dropped the cup. During those years growing up in school and at the monastery, Luther only thought of God’s righteousness, or justice, as his active judgment against human sin. He later wrote , Though I lived as a monk without reproach, I felt and knew I was a sinner before God. I had an extremely disturbed conscience. . . . I hated the righteous God who punishes sinners. 2. Extra nos In 1512, Luther became a university professor in Wittenberg. As he studied the Bible for his lectures, he began to see God’s righteousness in a new light. Luther saw how Jesus Christ took on our humanity, how he lived a perfect life and died the painful and shameful death of the cross to take the punishment due for sin. He saw how God raised Jesus from the dead, and how he now justifies Christians by faith. God declares that in his sight, Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift of salvation. Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift. What happened when Luther made this discovery? Here’s how he described it: “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” After that day, Luther began to teach that God gives Christians his “alien righteousness,” that is, a righteousness that comes extra nos , “from outside of us.” Our righteousness isn’t from us; it doesn’t come from what we do. It can’t be earned by saying a prayer or even by having a good attitude. Our righteousness is ultimately found in and belongs to another, our Savior Jesus Christ. 3. Crux sola est nostra theologia On October 31, 1517, Luther famously posted his Ninety-five Theses on the door of Castle Church. In it, Luther spoke clearly against the money-raising indulgence schemes Pope Leo X and Germany’s own Prince Albert of Brandenburg had sponsored. The next year, in April 1518, Luther defended these views at the Augustinian order’s spring meeting in Heidelberg. Luther walked to the meeting in fear. He expected the leaders there to sternly rebuke him. After all, that’s what the pope had asked them to do. But to Luther’s surprise, the leaders at the meeting welcomed his defense with excitement. What did Luther say that got his new friends so excited? In his Heidelberg Disputation , Luther described two types of people—the “theologian of glory” and the “theologian of the cross.” Theologians of glory think people are capable and smart enough to know God through human reason. They also say we can know who God’s righteous people are because we see God reward them with political power, success, and wealth. Though Luther didn’t use Albert’s and Leo’s names in his disputation, it’s clear he was talking about their greedy doctrine of indulgences when he described the theologian of glory. Luther’s “theologian of the cross,” by contrast, knows it’s not always people who appear good, beautiful, and powerful by worldly standards who truly know God. After all, Jesus didn’t look glorious on the cross. “One deserves to be called a true theologian,” Luther wrote , “who sees God even in suffering.” As Paul wrote, “God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). After Heidelberg, the phrase “ Crux sola est nostra theologia ” (“The cross alone is our theology”) became a rallying cry for Luther’s followers. It still is today. 4. Oratio, meditatio, tentatio Luther’s teaching set the Protestant Reformation in motion. In support of his reforms, Luther published hundreds of books, sermons, and hymns. Significantly, he also translated the entire Bible into the language of Germany’s common people. But Luther didn’t want common people to merely read Scripture. He wanted them to study it too. In the 1539 preface to the Wittenberg edition of his German writings, Luther wrote, “God himself lives in the Bible. Therefore, worthy Christian: get in, get in!” Luther gave his readers three rules for digging into God’s Word. Each has its own Latin term: prayer ( oratio ), meditation ( meditatio ), and suffering ( tentatio ). A ‘theologian of the cross’ knows it’s not always people who appear good, beautiful, and powerful by worldly standards who truly know God. The first rule is kept before we read the Bible. Luther wrote, “Kneel down in your private room and with humility, pray to God to give you his Holy Spirit to enlighten and guide and give you understanding.” The second rule is kept while reading: “Read and reread the very words written down in the Bible. Observe and think about what the Holy Spirit means.” The last rule is kept when we practice what the Scriptures say. Luther said, As soon as you begin to know God’s word, the devil will afflict you. . . . This suffering will teach you how right, true, sweet, lovely, mighty, and comforting God’s word is. It is wisdom supreme. 5. Simul iustus et peccator Luther was zealous and driven. He once said, “When I want to compose, write, pray, and preach well, I must be angry.” But while anger may have given Luther energy for work, it too often burned out of control. Sadly, today, Luther is as famous for his harsh words spoken against his enemies and the Jews as he is for recovering the biblical doctrine of justification. Throughout his life, Luther taught that believers are simul iustus et peccator . That’s Latin for “simultaneously justified and a sinner.” Both realities are true of every Christian. Both were true of Luther. He was a broken man who desperately needed God’s grace, and he knew it. Luther died while visiting Eisleben on February 18, 1546. Before he died, Luther scribbled out his last written words: “We are beggars. This is true.” Luther knew he could never earn God’s grace. Salvation isn’t won through indulgences or daily prayers. This is what Luther had discovered from the Bible and taught again to the world. God sent his only Son. Christ has overcome the world. All he asks of poor, begging sinners is that we believe.
